dervis-irab:34-37.t:
* I'rab:
(قالَتْ إِنَّ الْمُلُوكَ إِذا دَخَلُوا قَرْيَةً أَفْسَدُوها): resumptive speech, introduced to answer her counsellors; that is, she was not pleased with what they advised, namely entering into war, but inclined towards peace and concluding a truce, and she gave the reason for that with her words "Kings, …", as though she were hinting to them at the evil outcome of war, its fearful consequences and its many after-effects.
(إن) and its noun; (إذا) is an adverb of future time containing the meaning of condition; the clause (دخلوا) is in the position of the genitive by the annexation of the adverb to it; (قرية) is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object) by extension (ʿalā al-saʿa); the clause (أفسدوها) is the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) of a non-jussive condition and has no grammatical position; the conditional clause and its apodosis are the khabar (predicate) of (إن). (وَجَعَلُوا أَعِزَّةَ أَهْلِها أَذِلَّةً وَكَذلِكَ يَفْعَلُونَ): the wāw is a conjunction; (جعلوا) is a verb and its fāʿil (agent); (أعزة أهلها) is the first object of (جعلوا) and (أذلة) is the second object of (جعلوا); in (وكذلك) the wāw is a conjunction, because this is part of her speech, and (كذلك) is a naʿt (adjective) of an omitted maṣdar (verbal noun), parallels of which have preceded; she meant: this is their continuing custom and their fixed habit. (وَإِنِّي مُرْسِلَةٌ إِلَيْهِمْ بِهَدِيَّةٍ فَناظِرَةٌ بِمَ يَرْجِعُ الْمُرْسَلُونَ): (إن) and its noun, and (مرسلة) is its khabar; (إليهم) is attached to (مرسلة), and (بهدية) is also attached to (مرسلة); (فناظرة) is conjoined to (مرسلة); in (بم) the bāʾ is a preposition and (ما) is the interrogative whose alif has been dropped, in the position of the genitive by the bāʾ, and the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to (يرجع). It is not permissible to attach them to (ناظرة) as al-Ḥawfī parsed it, because the interrogative has the right to the head of the sentence, so what precedes it cannot govern it, otherwise it would depart from what is established for it. The exegetes have long discussions about this gift which the scope of this book cannot bear to mention. (يرجع المرسلون) is a verb and its agent, and the clause is the direct object of (ناظرة).
(فَلَمَّا جاءَ سُلَيْمانَ قالَ: أَتُمِدُّونَنِ بِمالٍ): the fāʾ conjoins to something omitted which must be supplied: "So she prepared the gift with a messenger carrying a letter"; further discussion of it will come in the Rhetoric section. (لما) is temporal (ḥīniyya), or a linking particle containing the meaning of condition; (جاء سليمان): (جاء) is a past verb and its agent is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "he", i.e. the messenger, and (سليمان) is the direct object; the clause (قال) has no grammatical position. The hamza is for disapproving, rebuking interrogation; (تمدونن) is an imperfect verb in the nominative (marfūʿ), the sign of its nominative being the retention of the nūn; the wāw is the agent, the nūn is the nūn of protection (wiqāya), and the dropped yāʾ is the direct object; (بمال) is attached to (تمدونن), i.e. "Do you help me with wealth?" (فَما آتانِيَ اللَّهُ خَيْرٌ مِمَّا آتاكُمْ بَلْ أَنْتُمْ بِهَدِيَّتِكُمْ تَفْرَحُونَ): the fāʾ is a particle of causation for his preceding disapproval of them and his rebuke of them; (ما) is a relative noun, mubtadaʾ (subject), and the clause (آتاني) is the ṣila (relative clause); (آتاني الله) is a past verb, a fronted direct object and a postponed agent; (خير) is the khabar of (ما). (بل) is a particle of transitional digression (iḍrāb intiqālī), to explain the cause that drove them to supply him with wealth; (أنتم) is a mubtadaʾ; (بهديتكم) is attached to (تفرحون), and the clause (تفرحون) is the khabar. (ارْجِعْ إِلَيْهِمْ فَلَنَأْتِيَنَّهُمْ بِجُنُودٍ لا قِبَلَ لَهُمْ بِها): the address is to the head of the delegation; (ارجع) is an imperative verb whose agent is latent, its implied form being "you"; (إليهم) is attached to (ارجع). It has been said that the address is to the hoopoe, charging it with another letter. The fāʾ is resumptive; the lām prepares for the oath (muwaṭṭiʾa lil-qasam); (نأتينهم) is an imperfect verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on the fatḥa because it is attached to the heavy nūn of emphasis; its agent is latent, its implied form being "we"; the hāʾ is the direct object and the mīm is the sign of the masculine plural; (بجنود) is attached to (نأتينهم). (لا) is the lā of generic negation, (قبل) is its indeclinable noun, and (لهم) is the khabar; (بها) is attached to (قبل) because it contains the meaning of a maṣdar, since its real sense is facing and resisting. One says: «مالي به قبل», i.e. "I have no power for it"; and one says «لي قبل فلان دين», i.e. "So-and-so owes me a debt" (lit. "with him"); and «أتاني من قبله», i.e. "from him". So it can have the sense of a maṣdar and the sense of an adverb. (وَلَنُخْرِجَنَّهُمْ مِنْها أَذِلَّةً وَهُمْ صاغِرُونَ): (ولنخرجنهم) is conjoined to (فلنأتينهم); (منها) is attached to (نخرجنهم), and the pronoun refers back to Sabaʾ, i.e. their land; (أذلة) is a ḥāl (circumstantial); in (وهم) the wāw is circumstantial and (هم) is a mubtadaʾ, (صاغرون) is the khabar, and the clause is a second ḥāl of the hāʾ in (لنخرجنهم).

* Rhetoric:
Concision (al-ījāz):
In these verses there is an eloquent concision which it is well for us to ponder, because the point in it turns on meanings rather than words; for many a short phrase enfolds abundant meaning. We have already seen that concision is of two kinds: one is concision by ellipsis (ījāz bil-ḥadhf), which is that from which a single element is omitted, and concision by compression (ījāz bil-qaṣr). In these verses there is concision by ellipsis, namely His words «بم يرجع المرسلون» and then His words «فلما جاء سليمان»; for here something has been omitted which, had it been made explicit, would have made the speech appear lean and unbefitting the charm and beauty it had at first, because the mind may go in every direction, and the imagination may be given free rein to roam in endless horizons to picture the gift she prepared, which the commentary undertakes to bring out. It is related that Bilqīs was an intelligent, sagacious woman who had managed affairs and sounded the depths of people, and she knew that if Solomon were a prophet he would disdain to accept the gift, and if he were a king he would take it, so she wished to make sure of this matter. It is also related that she sent five hundred young men wearing the clothes of slave-girls and their ornaments — bracelets, collars and earrings — riding horses covered with brocade, their bridles and saddles adorned with gold inlaid with jewels; and five hundred slave-girls on mares (rimāk, i.e. female horses) in the dress of young men; and a thousand bricks of gold and silver; and a crown studded with pearls and fine rubies; and musk and ambergris; and a casket containing an unpierced pearl and an onyx bead with a crooked bore. She sent two men from the nobles of her people, al-Mundhir ibn ʿAmr and another, men of intelligence and judgment, and then said to al-Mundhir: "If he looks at you with the look of an angry man, then he is a king, so do not let his affair frighten you; and if you see him cheerful and gentle, then he is a prophet." The hoopoe came and informed Solomon of what had taken place, so Solomon commanded the jinn, and they moulded bricks of gold and silver and laid them out in a square before him seven parasangs long, and they built around the square a wall with battlements of gold and silver. He commanded the finest beasts, and they tethered them on the right and left of the square, and he commanded the children of the jinn, a great multitude, and they lined up for parasangs on his right and left. When the people drew near and looked, they were dumbfounded. Then he returned the gift and said to al-Mundhir: "Return to them." She said: "He is a prophet, and we have no power against him," and she made ready to travel to Solomon to see what he would command her. She set out with twelve thousand qayl, i.e. kings — with a fatḥa on the qāf — called qayl because he executes all that he says, until she came within a parasang of him, and he perceived her.
Furthermore, hadiyya is a noun for the thing given as a gift, just as ʿaṭiyya is a noun for the thing given; so it may be annexed to the giver and to the recipient. You say "This is so-and-so's hadiyya", meaning the one he gave or the one given to him. The one annexed in His words «بل أنتم بهديتكم» is the recipient.

dervis-irab:38-44.t:
* Vocabulary:
(عِفْرِيتٌ): al-ʿifrīt is the wicked, abominable one who is effective in affairs together with cunning, and that is said of humans, jinn and devils; its plural is ʿafārīt and its feminine ʿifrīta; ʿifriya is the same, and it has been read thus. One says rajul ʿifriya, ʿifr and ʿifīr when he is sound, strong, of pleasing build; it is taken from ʿafar al-arḍ, which is dust, i.e. from one who throws his opponent into the dust. From it comes layth ʿifrīn, i.e. a lion among lions that rolls its prey in the dust. Al-Khalīl said: rajul ʿifār, manifest in ʿafāra, when described as devilish. Al-ʿifīr is also the witty, clever one. The devil is called ʿifrīt and ʿifriya. In the ḥadīth: «إن الله ليبغض العفريت النفريت» ("Allah hates the ʿifrīt nifrīt"); it was said that this is the one who hoards and withholds. Abū ʿUthmān al-Nahdī said: A big man came in to the Prophet ﷺ and he said to him: "When did you last have a fever?" He said: "I do not know it." He said: "And a headache?" He said: "I do not know what it is." He said: "Have you been afflicted in your wealth?" He said: "No." He said: "Have you been bereaved of a child?" He said: "No." So the Prophet ﷺ said: "Allah hates the ʿifrīt nifrīt," and he is the one who suffers no loss.
(الصَّرْحَ): In al-Kashshāf he said: al-ṣarḥ is «the palace; and it is said: the courtyard of the house». Its origin is from taṣrīḥ, which is uncovering; kadhib ṣurāḥ is an evident, exposed lie, and luʾm ṣurāḥ (open baseness); laban ṣarīḥ is milk whose froth has gone and which has become pure; ʿarabī ṣarīḥ, of ʿarab ṣuraḥāʾ, means not of mixed descent; kaʾs ṣurāḥ is an unmixed cup; ṣarraḥat al-khamra: its foam went away; laqītuhu muṣāraḥatan: openly; ṣarraḥa al-nahār: its clouds went away and its sun shone. Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said, describing a wolf:
إذا امتلّ يعدو قلت ظلّ طخاءة ... ذرى الريح في أعقاب يوم مصرح
(When it sets off running, you would say it is the shadow of a thin cloud scattered by the wind at the end of a day that has cleared.)
(مُمَرَّدٌ): al-mumarrad is that which is made smooth; the secret of its form will come in the Benefits section [Translator's note: no such discussion appears in the Benefits section of this entry]. From it comes al-amrad (the beardless youth), because of the smoothness of his face, i.e. its softness, owing to the absence of hair on it. In al-Qāmūs: «al-tamrīd in building is smoothing and levelling; and a bināʾ mumarrad is one made tall; and al-mārid is the lofty and the insolent».
(قَوارِيرَ): In al-Miṣbāḥ: «The qārūra is a vessel of glass, plural qawārīr; qārūra is also a container for fresh dates and dried dates, namely the qawṣara. Qārūra is applied to a woman, because the child or the semen settles (yaqirru) in her womb as a thing settles in a vessel, or by comparison with glass vessels because of her weakness. Al-Azharī said: The Arabs allude to a woman by qārūra and qawṣara.» In al-Qāmūs: «The qārūra is the pupil of the eye, and that in which drink or the like settles, or it is restricted to glass; and qawārīr min fiḍḍa means of glass with the whiteness of silver and the clarity of glass.»

* I'rab:
(قالَ يا أَيُّهَا الْمَلَؤُا أَيُّكُمْ يَأْتِينِي بِعَرْشِها قَبْلَ أَنْ يَأْتُونِي مُسْلِمِينَ): the fāʿil (agent) of (قال) is Solomon, and the address is to everyone who was with him of the jinn, humans and others. (أيكم) is a mubtadaʾ (subject) and the clause (يأتيني بعرشها) is the khabar (predicate); the adverb is also attached to (يأتيني); (أن) and what falls in its domain is an interpreted maṣdar, muḍāf ilayhi; (مسلمين) is a ḥāl (circumstantial).
(قالَ عِفْرِيتٌ مِنَ الْجِنِّ أَنَا آتِيكَ بِهِ قَبْلَ أَنْ تَقُومَ مِنْ مَقامِكَ): (قال) is a past verb and (عفريت) is the agent; (من الجن) is an adjective; (أنا) is a mubtadaʾ and the clause (آتيك به) is the khabar; the adverb is attached to (آتيك); (من مقامك) is attached to (تقوم), i.e. before you leave your sitting-place in which you sit for judgment from early morning until midday.
(وَإِنِّي عَلَيْهِ لَقَوِيٌّ أَمِينٌ): the wāw is a conjunction; (إن) and its noun; (عليه) is attached to (قوي); the lām is the shifted lām (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa); (قوي) is the khabar and (أمين) a second khabar; i.e. strong enough to carry it, trustworthy with it: I will not purloin anything from it nor tamper with it. (قالَ الَّذِي عِنْدَهُ عِلْمٌ مِنَ الْكِتابِ: أَنَا آتِيكَ بِهِ قَبْلَ أَنْ يَرْتَدَّ إِلَيْكَ طَرْفُكَ): something omitted must be supplied by way of concision, as before, namely: Solomon said, "I want that to be done in the shortest time." (قال) is a past verb and (الذي) is the agent; the adverb is attached to an omitted fronted khabar and (علم) is a postponed mubtadaʾ; (من الكتاب) is an adjective of (علم), and the clause is the ṣila (relative clause) of the relative noun. (أنا) is a mubtadaʾ and the clause (آتيك به) is the khabar, and the clause is the object of saying (maqūl al-qawl). The parsing of the rest has preceded, and the meaning of the returning of the glance will come in the Rhetoric section. (فَلَمَّا رَآهُ مُسْتَقِرًّا عِنْدَهُ قالَ هذا مِنْ فَضْلِ رَبِّي): the fāʾ conjoins to something omitted, to be supplied according to the context. It is related that Āṣaf ibn Barkhiyā — he is the one who had knowledge of the revealed Book — said to Solomon: "Extend your eyes until your glance reaches its limit." So Solomon extended his eyes and looked towards Yemen, and Āṣaf prayed with the knowledge he had, and the throne sank in its place at Maʾrib and then emerged in Solomon's assembly. (لما) is an adverb meaning "when", or a linking particle; (رآه) is a verb, a latent agent and a direct object; (مستقرا) is a ḥāl, because the seeing is visual, i.e. firmly set; the adverb is attached to (مستقرا); the clause (قال) has no grammatical position; (هذا) is a mubtadaʾ and (من فضل ربي) is the khabar.
(لِيَبْلُوَنِي أَأَشْكُرُ أَمْ أَكْفُرُ): the lām is for causation; (يبلوني) is an imperfect verb in the accusative by an implied (muḍmara) an after the lām of causation; the agent of (يبلوني) refers back to (ربي), and the yāʾ is the object. In (أأشكر) the hamza is for interrogation, and (أشكر) is an imperfect verb whose agent is latent, its implied form being "I"; the clause (أأشكر) is a badal (substitute) of the yāʾ in (يبلوني), so it stands as the direct object; (أم أكفر) is conjoined to (أأشكر). (وَمَنْ شَكَرَ فَإِنَّما يَشْكُرُ لِنَفْسِهِ وَمَنْ كَفَرَ فَإِنَّ رَبِّي غَنِيٌّ كَرِيمٌ): the wāw is resumptive; (من) is conditional, a mubtadaʾ; (شكر) is a past verb in the position of the jussive as the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ); the fāʾ is a linking particle because the apodosis is a nominal clause; (إن) is a particle resembling the verb and (ما) is maṣdariyya, and it together with what follows is in the sense of a maṣdar, the noun of (إن), i.e. "the reward of his thanks"; (لنفسه) is the khabar. The protasis and its apodosis are the khabar of (من). (ومن كفر فإن ربي غني كريم) is a clause conjoined to the preceding clause and parallel to it in parsing. [Translator's note: the verse reads «فَإِنَّما يَشْكُرُ لِنَفْسِهِ»; the parsing given here treats (إنما) as إنّ + maṣdariyya ما with (لنفسه) as khabar, and does not mention the verb (يشكر). It is translated as written.] (قالَ: نَكِّرُوا لَها عَرْشَها نَنْظُرْ أَتَهْتَدِي أَمْ تَكُونُ مِنَ الَّذِينَ لا يَهْتَدُونَ): (نكروا) is an imperative verb and the wāw is the agent; (لها) is attached to (نكروا); (عرشها) is the direct object, i.e. alter it. (ننظر) is an imperfect verb in the jussive (majzūm) because it is the answer to the command; it was read in the nominative as resumptive. The clause (أتهتدي) is in the position of the accusative as object, because the interrogative has suspended (ʿallaqa) (ننظر) from governing. (أم) is a conjunction balancing the hamza; (تكون) is an incomplete imperfect verb conjoined to (أتهتدي); its noun is latent, its implied form being "she"; (من الذين) is the khabar of (تكون), and the clause (لا يهتدون) is the ṣila of (الذين). (فَلَمَّا جاءَتْ قِيلَ أَهكَذا عَرْشُكِ قالَتْ كَأَنَّهُ هُوَ): the fāʾ conjoins to something omitted, required by concision as before. (أهكذا): the hamza is for interrogation, the hāʾ is for drawing attention (tanbīh), the kāf is a preposition of comparison, and (ذا) is a demonstrative in the position of the genitive by the kāf; the preposition and its genitive noun are a fronted khabar and (عرشك) is a postponed mubtadaʾ. The basic form is for the hāʾ of attention to be joined to the demonstrative, so it would have required saying «أكهذا عرشك؟». This separation is permissible when the preposition is a kāf; if you said «أبهذا أمرت» or «ألهذا فعلت؟», that separation would not be permissible in it, so you may not say «أها بذا أمرت» and «أها لذا فعلت؟». The secret of bringing the kāf of comparison and not being content with saying «أهذا عرشك» will come in the Rhetoric section. (قالت) is a verb and a latent agent, its implied form being "she", referring to Bilqīs; (كأنه هو): (كأن) and its noun, and the pronoun (هو) is its khabar. The secret of her turning away from making the answer match the question will also come in the Rhetoric section.
(وَأُوتِينَا الْعِلْمَ مِنْ قَبْلِها وَكُنَّا مُسْلِمِينَ): the wāw conjoins to speech omitted for concision, i.e. when they heard her saying «كأنه هو» they said: "She has answered correctly", and Solomon said «وأوتينا». It is a passive past verb and (نا) is the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent); (العلم) is the second object of (أوتينا); (من قبلها) is attached to (أوتينا); in (وكنا) the wāw is a conjunction, and (كان) and its noun, and (مسلمين) is its khabar. It is possible that (وأوتينا) is part of Bilqīs's speech, in which case the pronoun in (قبلها) refers to the miracle and the situation indicated by the context of the speech, the meaning being: "We were given knowledge of Solomon's prophethood before the appearance of this miracle", or "before this situation". The first is preferable.
(وَصَدَّها ما كانَتْ تَعْبُدُ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ إِنَّها كانَتْ مِنْ قَوْمٍ كافِرِينَ): part of Solomon's speech or of Allah's speech. (صدها) is a past verb and a direct object; (ما) is a relative noun, the agent; the clause (كانت) is the ṣila; the noun of (كانت) is latent, its implied form being "she", and the clause (تعبد) is the khabar; (من دون الله) is a ḥāl. It is permissible for (ما) to be maṣdariyya, i.e. her worship of the sun barred her from Islam. The clause (إنها) gives the reason for the barring from Islam and the worship of other than Allah; (إن) and its noun, and the clause (كانت) is its khabar; the noun of (كانت) is "she" and (من قوم) is its khabar, and (كافرين) is an adjective. It was read «أنها» with fatḥa, as a badal of the agent of (صدها), or accusative by removal of the preposition. (قِيلَ لَهَا ادْخُلِي الصَّرْحَ): (قيل) is a passive past verb and the clause is resumptive; the clause (ادخلي الصرح) is the object of saying; (الصرح) is a direct object by extension. The story of the palace will come in the Benefits section. (فَلَمَّا رَأَتْهُ حَسِبَتْهُ لُجَّةً وَكَشَفَتْ عَنْ ساقَيْها): the fāʾ conjoins to something omitted for concision, i.e. "so she entered it"; (لما) is temporal or a linking particle; the clause (حسبته) has no grammatical position; the hāʾ is the first direct object and (لجة) the second direct object; (وكشفت عن ساقيها) is conjoined to (حسبته). (قالَ إِنَّهُ صَرْحٌ مُمَرَّدٌ مِنْ قَوارِيرَ): (إن) and its noun, and (صرح) is its khabar; (ممرد) is an adjective, and (من قوارير) a second adjective; i.e. what you thought to be water — above it is a smoothed palace, i.e. roofed with a surface, so whoever wishes to cross it does not need to tuck up his clothes. (قالَتْ رَبِّ إِنِّي ظَلَمْتُ نَفْسِي وَأَسْلَمْتُ مَعَ سُلَيْمانَ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعالَمِينَ): (رب) is a vocative muḍāf from which the vocative particle has been omitted; (إن) and its noun, and the clause (ظلمت نفسي) is its khabar; (أسلمت) is conjoined to (ظلمت); (مع) is an adverb of place attached to an omitted ḥāl, i.e. "being with Solomon". It was supplied as a ḥāl only because attaching it to (أسلمت) would suggest that their two submissions coincided in time. (لله) is attached to (أسلمت), and (رب العالمين) is a badal of (الله) or an adjective of it.

* Rhetoric:
1- Metonymy in the returning of the glance:
In His words «قبل أن يرتد إليك طرفك» there is kināya (metonymy) for speed. Al-ṭarf is the movement of your eyelids when you look; it was put in place of looking, and since the looker is described as sending out the glance, he is described as returning the glance, and the glance is described as returning. On that pattern is the saying:
وكنت إذا أرسلت طرفك رائدا ... لقبلك يوما أتعبتك المناظر
رأيت الذي لاكله أنت قادر ... عليه ولا عن بعضه أنت صابر
(Whenever you sent your glance out one day as a scout for your heart, the sights wearied you: you saw that of which you are not capable of the whole, nor patient to forgo a part.)
These two verses are by a Bedouin woman whom a Bedouin man looked at and addressed with poetry asking her about her circumstances and her charms, as if trying to seduce her, and she answered him with that; it is also said to be by a poet of the Ḥamāsa. Letting the sight loose towards beautiful sights is likened to sending the scout ahead of the caravan to find for them the place of pasture, by way of explicit metaphor (istiʿāra taṣrīḥiyya); (رائدا) is a reinforcement (tarshīḥ) of the metaphor, and (يوما) is an adverb for it.
2- The secret in the simile:
In her words «كأنه هو» there is an unqualified simile (tashbīh mursal) to which she turned away from what the question required — and it required that she say "It is it" — for a very subtle secret. That is that «كأنه» is an expression of one with whom the resemblance is so close that he has made himself doubt the difference between the two things, so that he almost says "It is it"; and that was Bilqīs's state. Since "It is thus" is the expression of one certain of the difference between the two things, judging only that resemblance occurs between them, she therefore turned to the expression mentioned in the recitation, because it matched her state. [Translator's note: the phrase «ولما كانت هكذا هو» is translated as written; the sense appears to be that «هكذا هو» would have expressed certainty of difference.]
3- Paronomasia (al-tajnīs):
It is the agreement of two words in the arrangement of their letters, and here it is in His words «وأسلمت مع سليمان».

* Benefits:
1- The story of the palace:
Furthermore, we summarise what is related of the story of the palace, since it is a poetic story of soaring imagination. It is related that Solomon gave orders before her arrival, and there was built for him on her way a palace of white glass; he made water flow beneath it and cast into it sea creatures, fish and others, and he placed his throne at its head and sat upon it. When she saw the deep water she was alarmed and thought that he intended to drown her, and she was amazed that his seat was upon the water, but she had no choice but to obey the command, so she uncovered her shins. The purpose of all this was to test her intelligence and to herald the miracles to her — not what is related, that he was told that she had hairy shins and that her foot was like a donkey's hoof, which does not accord with the dignity of prophethood and its elevation above petty things.
2- Did Solomon marry Bilqīs?
It is said that he married her after that and confirmed her in her kingdom, and he would visit her once a month and stay with her three days, and she bore him children. And it is said rather that he married her to Dhū Tubbaʿ, one of the kings of Yemen, who are called al-Adhwāʾ because their names are headed by the word (ذو), meaning "the possessor of" this name.

dervis-irab:45-53.t:
* Vocabulary:
(اطَّيَّرْنا): taṭayyarnā means: we took an evil omen. Al-ṭāʾir here is that from which you take a good omen or an evil omen, and the second is what is meant here. A man would go out on a journey and pass by a bird and scare it off: if it passed from left to right (sāniḥ) he took a good omen, and if it passed from right to left (bāriḥ) he took an evil omen. Since they attributed good or evil to the bird, the word was borrowed for what was the cause of these from Allah's decree and apportionment, or from the servant's deeds. This has passed in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf, so renew your acquaintance with it.
(الْمَدِينَةِ): the town. Whoever derives it from madana bil-makān yamdunu, when one resides in a place, takes it as faʿīla, its plural being madāʾin with hamza, the mīm being a root letter and the yāʾ extra. Whoever derives it from dāna yadīnu takes the mīm as extra and the yāʾ as a root letter, and it is mafʿūla. One says dintu al-rajula, "I owned the man", and dintu lahu, "I submitted to him and obeyed"; and the slave-woman is called madīna because she is owned. The poet said:
ثوت وثوى في كرمها ابن مدينة ... يظل على مسحاته يتوكل
(She stayed, and in her vineyard stayed the son of a slave-woman, who keeps leaning on his spade.)
In the dictionaries of the language: madana bil-makān yamdunu, of the naṣara pattern, mudūnan: he resided; it is an obsolete verb. Madana al-madīna: he came to it; maddana al-madāʾin with doubling: he built them and made them cities. Tamaddana: he took on the manners of the city-dwellers and moved from savagery to a state of sociability and refinement. Madīna is pluralised as mudn with sukūn on the dāl, mudun with ḍamma on it, and madāʾin. Al-Madīna is a proper name applied to Yathrib; Madīnat al-Salām is Baghdad; and al-Madāʾin is a city near Baghdad in which was the Īwān of Khosrow, named with the plural because of its size, and the relative adjective from it is Madāʾinī.
(رَهْطٍ): al-rahṭ is a man's people and his tribe, and a number gathered from three to ten among whom there is no woman; it has no singular from its own root; its plural is arhuṭ and arhāṭ, and the plural of the plural arāhiṭ and arāhīṭ. When a number is annexed to rahṭ, what is meant by it is the person and the individual, as in "twenty rahṭ", i.e. twenty persons. One says "We are dhawū rahṭ", i.e. gathered together. In al-Miṣbāḥ: «al-rahṭ is fewer than ten men among whom there is no woman; the sukūn on the hāʾ is more eloquent than its fatḥa; it is a plural with no singular from its own root. It is said that rahṭ is from seven to ten, and fewer than seven down to three is nafar. Abū Zayd said: rahṭ and nafar are fewer than ten men. Thaʿlab also said: rahṭ, nafar, qawm, maʿshar and ʿashīra — their meaning is a group; they have no singular from their own root, and it is for men to the exclusion of women. Ibn al-Sikkīt said: rahṭ and ʿitra have one meaning. And it is said: rahṭ is what is above ten up to forty — al-Aṣmaʿī said it, and Ibn Fāris also transmitted it. A man's rahṭ is his people and his nearest tribe.» Further discussion of it will come in the I'rab section. [Translator's note: the further discussion actually appears in the Benefits section.]

* I'rab:
(وَلَقَدْ أَرْسَلْنا إِلى ثَمُودَ أَخاهُمْ صالِحاً أَنِ اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ): resumptive speech, introduced to set out the third story — or the fourth, if the story of the ants is taken separately from the story of Solomon and Bilqīs — which is the story of Ṣāliḥ. The lām is the answer to an omitted oath; (قد) is a particle of verification; (أرسلنا) is a past verb and its fāʿil (agent); (إلى ثمود) is attached to (أرسلنا); (أخاهم) is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object); (صالحا) is a badal (substitute) of (أخاهم) or an ʿaṭf bayān (explicative apposition). (أن) is maṣdariyya, and it with what it enters upon is in the sense of a maṣdar (verbal noun) that is accusative by removal of the preposition; it is also correct for it to be explicative (mufassira), because sending contains the meaning of saying. (اعبدوا الله) is an imperative verb, an agent and a direct object. (فَإِذا هُمْ فَرِيقانِ يَخْتَصِمُونَ): the fāʾ is a conjunction; (إذا) is the (إذا) of surprise, about which discussion has preceded; (هم) is a mubtadaʾ (subject) and (فريقان) the khabar (predicate); the clause (يختصمون) is a naʿt (adjective) of (فريقان) according to the sense, like the saying of Allah the Exalted «وان طائفتان من المؤمنين اقتتلوا», because each party comprises a group. (قالَ يا قَوْمِ لِمَ تَسْتَعْجِلُونَ بِالسَّيِّئَةِ قَبْلَ الْحَسَنَةِ): (يا) is a vocative particle and (قوم) is the one addressed, annexed to the omitted yāʾ of the speaker; in (لم) the lām is a preposition and (ما) is an interrogative noun whose alif was dropped because of the entry of the preposition; the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to (تستعجلون); (بالسيئة) is attached to (تستعجلون); (قبل الحسنة) is an adverb attached to an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial). What is meant by al-sayyiʾa is the punishment and by al-ḥasana the mercy, as will come. (لَوْلا تَسْتَغْفِرُونَ اللَّهَ لَعَلَّكُمْ تُرْحَمُونَ): (لولا) is a particle of urging (taḥḍīḍ) meaning "why not"; (تستغفرون الله) is an imperfect verb in the nominative (marfūʿ), the wāw is the agent and the Glorious Name is its object; (لعلكم ترحمون): (لعل) and its noun, and the clause is its khabar. (قالُوا اطَّيَّرْنا بِكَ وَبِمَنْ مَعَكَ): (اطيرنا) is a past verb and its agent; its original form is taṭayyarnā; the tāʾ was assimilated into the ṭāʾ, and the connecting hamza was brought in to make it possible to pronounce the vowelless letter, because the assimilated letter is always vowelless. (بك) is attached to (اطيرنا); (وبمن) is conjoined to (بك); (معك) is an adverb of place attached to an omitted ṣila (relative clause) of (من); and the clause is the object of their saying.
(قالَ طائِرُكُمْ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ بَلْ أَنْتُمْ قَوْمٌ تُفْتَنُونَ): (طائركم) is a mubtadaʾ and (عند الله) is an adverb attached to something omitted which is the khabar, and the clause is the object of his saying. (بل) is a particle of digression (iḍrāb): he digressed from explaining their omen, which is the origin of what befalls them, to mentioning what is the cause leading to it. (أنتم) is a mubtadaʾ and (قوم) the khabar, and the clause (تفتنون) is a naʿt of (قوم).
(وَكانَ فِي الْمَدِينَةِ تِسْعَةُ رَهْطٍ يُفْسِدُونَ فِي الْأَرْضِ وَلا يُصْلِحُونَ): the wāw is resumptive; (كان) is an incomplete past verb; (في المدينة) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to an omitted fronted khabar of (كان); (تسعة) is its postponed noun and (رهط) is muḍāf ilayhi. The discussion of the tamyīz (specification) of numbers will come in detail in the Benefits section. The clause (يفسدون) is an adjective of (تسعة), and (ولا يصلحون) is conjoined to (يفسدون). The secret of His saying «ولا يصلحون» will come in the Rhetoric section. (قالُوا تَقاسَمُوا بِاللَّهِ لَنُبَيِّتَنَّهُ وَأَهْلَهُ): (تقاسموا) is an imperative verb, i.e. swear. It may be a past verb, in which case it may be explicative, as if it were said: "What did they say?" and it were said: "They swore to one another"; and it may, with its agent, be a clause in the position of the accusative as a ḥāl, i.e. "they said, swearing to one another", with qad implied. Taqāsum and taqassum, like taẓāhur and taẓahhur, mean swearing mutual oaths. (لنبيتنه): the lām occurs in the answer to the oath; (نبيتنه) is from al-bayāt (a night attack), whose meaning has preceded elsewhere; it is an imperfect verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on the fatḥa because it is attached to the heavy nūn of emphasis; the agent is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "we"; the hāʾ is the direct object, i.e. we will surely take him by surprise at night. In (وأهله) the wāw is a conjunction and (أهله) is conjoined to the hāʾ; it may be parsed as a mafʿūl maʿahu (object of accompaniment), the wāw then being for accompaniment. (ثُمَّ لَنَقُولَنَّ لِوَلِيِّهِ ما شَهِدْنا مَهْلِكَ أَهْلِهِ وَإِنَّا لَصادِقُونَ): (ثم) is a conjunction for delay; the lām prepares for the oath (muwaṭṭiʾa lil-qasam); the parsing of the like of (نقولن) has preceded; (لوليه) is attached to (نقولن), i.e. those who have authority over his blood. (مهلك) is the direct object, and it is either a mīmī maṣdar, a noun of time or a noun of place; it was read with ḍamma on the mīm and fatḥa on the lām, as being from the quadriliteral; (أهله) is muḍāf ilayhi. [Translator's note: the source does not parse (ما شهدنا) itself — (ما) negative and (شهدنا) verb and agent, the clause being the object of (نقولن).] In (وإنا) the wāw is a conjunction or circumstantial; (إنا): (إن) and its noun; the lām is the shifted lām (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa) and (صادقون) is the khabar of (إن).
(وَمَكَرُوا مَكْراً وَمَكَرْنا مَكْراً وَهُمْ لا يَشْعُرُونَ): the wāw is a conjunction; (مكروا) is a verb and its agent; (مكرا) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object); (ومكرنا مكرا) is conjoined to the preceding clause; the wāw is circumstantial, (هم) is a mubtadaʾ and the clause (لا يشعرون) is the khabar. (فَانْظُرْ كَيْفَ كانَ عاقِبَةُ مَكْرِهِمْ أَنَّا دَمَّرْناهُمْ وَقَوْمَهُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ): the fāʾ is resumptive, and the speech is resumptive, introduced to show what resulted from their night plot and their base conspiracy; for a night attack is among the things found abhorrent. It is related of Alexander that a night attack was suggested to him, and he said: "Stealing victory is not of the āyīn of kings", i.e. of their custom and ways.
(كيف) is the fronted khabar of (كان) and (عاقبة) is the postponed noun of (كان); the clause is in the position of the accusative by removal of the preposition, and the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to (انظر), which is suspended from governing by the interrogative. (إنا) is a resumptive clause, and for that reason the hamza of (إنا) is given kasra; it was read with fatḥa, the maṣdar being a badal of (العاقبة) or the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ. (إن) and its noun, and the clause (دمرناهم) is its khabar; (أجمعين) is a tawkīd (emphasis) of each of the conjoined and what it is conjoined to. [Translator's note: the source here adds «أي صالح وأهله المؤمنين به وكانوا كما يروى أربعة آلاف», "i.e. Ṣāliḥ and his family who believed in him, and they were, as is related, four thousand"; in context this explanation evidently belongs to those who were saved (verse 53), not to those destroyed. It is translated as written.]
(فَتِلْكَ بُيُوتُهُمْ خاوِيَةً بِما ظَلَمُوا إِنَّ فِي ذلِكَ لَآيَةً لِقَوْمٍ يَعْلَمُونَ): the fāʾ is a conjunction, and the clause is conjoined to what precedes it, confirming it; (تلك) is a mubtadaʾ and (بيوتهم) the khabar; (خاوية) is a ḥāl of (بيوتهم), and what governs it is the sense of pointing; (بما ظلموا) is attached to (خاوية); (ما) is maṣdariyya and the bāʾ is causal, i.e. because of their wrongdoing. (إن) is a particle resembling the verb; (في ذلك) is its fronted khabar; the lām is the shifted lām and (آية) is its noun; (لقوم) is an adjective of (آية), and the clause (يعلمون) is an adjective of (قوم). (وَأَنْجَيْنَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا وَكانُوا يَتَّقُونَ): a verb, an agent and a direct object; the clause (آمنوا) is the ṣila; (وكانوا يتقون) is conjoined to (آمنوا), so it is within the domain of the ṣila; (كان), its noun and its khabar.

* Rhetoric:
1- Completion (al-tamām or al-tatmīm):
In His words «ولا يصلحون» there is the device of tamām, as Qudāma named it in Naqd al-Shiʿr, Ibn Rashīq in al-ʿUmda and Ibn ʿAsākir in al-Ṣināʿatayn [Translator's note: the author of Kitāb al-Ṣināʿatayn is Abū Hilāl al-ʿAskarī; the source has «ابن عساكر»], or tatmīm, as al-Ḥātimī named it. Its mention has preceded in al-Baqara and al-Naḥl, and we repeat its definition briefly here: it is that a word is brought into the speech such that, if it were removed from it, its meaning would be deficient in itself or in its qualities, though its wording is complete. For His words «وكان في المدينة تسعة رهط يفسدون في الأرض» — their concern was sheer corruption, and they were, as is related, insolent and harsh, and they were the ones who advised hamstringing the she-camel in order to spite Ṣāliḥ and provoke his anger; among them was Qudār ibn Sālif, famous for ill-omen, whose mention has preceded. But His words «يفسدون في الأرض» do not exclude that some good might rarely come from them or from one of them, so the speech was completed with His words «ولا يصلحون», to ward off that excuse from arising, or any doubt from entering some minds that it would arise; and thereby every hope of setting their affair right and of their condition improving was cut off.
2- Correspondence (al-mushākala):
In His words «ومكروا مكرا ومكرنا مكرا» there is the device of mushākala, which is mentioning a thing with the word of something else because it occurs in its company; for Allah is too holy for "scheming" (makr) to be used of Him, except that it is used here by way of mushākala. It is frequent in the Qur'an, and from it is «تعلم ما في نفسي ولا أعلم ما في نفسك», while the word nafs is not used of Allah, exalted and holy is He. As for their scheming, it is what they plotted at night against Ṣāliḥ and what they intended of destroying him and his family. As for Allah's scheming, it is His destroying them from where they did not perceive, by way of metaphor joined to mushākala: destruction is likened to scheming in its being harm done in secret, because the real meaning of scheming is entrapping others intentionally by way of treachery and stratagem. The story of their destruction has preceded in al-Shuʿabāʾ [Translator's note: so in the source, «الشعب»; presumably Sūrat al-Shuʿarāʾ is meant].

* Benefits:
1- The tamyīz (specification) of numbers:
The specifier of three to ten and what lies between them, if it is a generic noun (ism jins) — that is, one distinguished from its singular by the tāʾ, like shajar and tamr — or a collective noun (ism jamʿ) — that is, one indicating a plural that has no singular from its own root, like qawm and rahṭ — is put in the genitive by min. You say: "three of the dates (thalāthatun min al-tamr) I ate", "ten of the people I met", "nine of the group I accompanied". The Exalted said: «فخذ أربعة من الطير». It may be put in the genitive by annexing the number to it: the collective noun, as in the preceding verse «وكان في المدينة تسعة رهط», and in the ḥadīth: «ليس فيما دون خمس ذود صدقة» ("There is no alms-due on fewer than five dhawd [camels]"). The poet said:
ثلاثة أنفس وثلاث ذود ... لقد جار الزمان على عيالي
(Three souls and three camels — time has indeed been unjust to my family.)
Al-dhawd of camels is between three and ten; it is feminine and has no singular from its own root, as in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. Al-anfus is the plural of nafs, which is feminine; its number was made feminine [i.e. given the tāʾ] while the rule required it to be masculine [i.e. without the tāʾ] [Translator's note: the bracketed clarifications are added; the source speaks of "making its number feminine" and "the rule being to make it masculine" in the reversed gender-agreement sense of numerals], because nafs is much used with the human being as what is meant. As for the generic noun, it is like the saying of Jandal ibn al-Muthannā:
كأن خصييه من التدلدل ... ظرف عجوز فيه ثنتا حنظل
(As if his testicles, from their dangling, were an old woman's bag containing two colocynths.)
(حنظل) is a generic noun in the genitive by annexation, in the manner of «تسعة رهط». Furthermore, in place of al-tadaldul is related al-tahaddul, which is better, and also "saḥq jirāb" (a worn-out bag). He specified the old woman because she does not use perfume, such that there would be something in her bag with which to adorn herself. The verse is among the most obscene invective.
If the specifier of three to ten and what lies between them is a plural, it is put in the genitive by annexing the number to it, as in thalāthatu rijālin and thalāthu imāʾin. Masculine and feminine are reckoned with collective and generic nouns according to their state in respect of the pronoun referring to them, masculine or feminine; the number is given the reverse of what their pronoun is entitled to. If their pronoun is masculine the number is made feminine, and if it is feminine it is made masculine. So you say with the generic noun «ثلاثة من الغنم عندي», with the tāʾ in thalātha, because you say «غنم كثير» with the masculine for the pronoun latent in kathīr. The author of al-Miṣbāḥ related that with ghanam its pronoun may be masculine or feminine. And «ثلاث من البط», omitting the tāʾ from thalāth, because you say «بط كثيرة» with the feminine for the pronoun latent in kathīr. And «ثلاثة» or «ثلاث من البقر», because the pronoun of baqar may be masculine or feminine, since there are two usages for baqar, masculine and feminine. Allah the Exalted said: «إن البقر تشابه علينا» with a masculine pronoun, and it was read «تشابهت» with it feminine. As for the collective noun, its rule is that of the masculine if it is for rational beings, like al-qawm, al-rahṭ and al-nafar, and if it is for non-rational beings its rule is that of the feminine, like al-jāmil (a herd of camels) and al-bāqir (a herd of cattle). This is what the grammarians mentioned, but there is a reservation about it, because niswa is a collective noun and its rule is that of the feminine by agreement, so one says «ثلاث نسوة».
Masculine and feminine with a plural are reckoned by the state of its singular: if its singular is masculine its number is made feminine, and if it is feminine its number is made masculine. Therefore you say «ثلاثة اصطبلات», plural of iṣṭabl with a disjunctive hamza with kasra, and «ثلاثة حمامات», because al-iṣṭabl and al-ḥammām are masculine; and you say «ثلاث سحابات», omitting the tāʾ, by reference to saḥāba, which is feminine. Of the state of the singular, the state of its wording is not taken into account, such that one would say «ثلاث طلحات» omitting the tāʾ; nor is the state of its meaning taken into account, such that one would say «ثلاث أشخص», likewise omitting it, meaning women, since shakhṣ applies to male and female; rather one looks at what the singular is entitled to with respect to its pronoun, and reverses its rule in the number. As for the saying of ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa:
فكان مجني دون من كنت أتقي ... ثلاث شخوص كاعبان ومعصر
(My shield against those I feared was three figures: two full-breasted girls and a girl come of age.)
it is poetic licence; the rule would have been «ثلاثة شخوص» with the tāʾ, but he alluded to women by al-shukhūṣ, and what made that easy was his words «كاعبان ومعصر», so the wording was joined to what supports the intended meaning, namely the feminine. Al-kāʿib is the girl when her breasts begin to swell, and al-muʿṣir, with ḍamma on the mīm and kasra on the ṣād, is the girl when she first reaches maturity, called that because she has entered the age (ʿaṣr) of youth, as al-Khalīl said.
Furthermore, the reins of speech have run away with us, so what has preceded is sufficient for us; we have brought it for its importance and benefit, and whoever wants more must refer to the lengthy works.
2- Know that they have formed broken plurals of some nouns not on the singular in use; rather they took another word synonymous with it and formed the broken plural on what is not used. Among that is rahṭ and arāhiṭ. The poet said:
يا بؤس للحرب التي ... وضعت أراهط فاستراحوا
(Oh, the misery of war, which brought down noble clans, and they were at rest!)
It is not regular for rahṭ to be pluralised as arāhiṭ, because this form is among the plurals of the quadriliteral and what has its number of letters, like jaʿfar and jaʿāfir, jadwal and jadāwil, arnab and arānib. Arhuṭ is not the plural of rahṭ [Translator's note: as written; the sense of the argument appears to be that arāhiṭ is not the plural of arhuṭ]; for if it were so it would not be irregular. What shows that is that the poet brought it when he needed it, saying:
وفاضح مفتضح في أرهطه ... من أرفع الوادي ولا من بعثطه
(A disgracer, himself disgraced among his clans — not from the highest part of the valley, nor from its best ground.)
Al-buʿthuṭ and al-buʿthūṭ: the navel (centre) of the valley and the best place in it.
Furthermore, the grammarians differed over arāhiṭ: some of them claimed that it is the plural of arhuṭ, which is the plural of rahṭ, which is the group of three to ten; most of the grammarians claimed that arāhiṭ is the plural of rahṭ contrary to rule. The verse is the opening of an ode by Saʿd ibn Mālik ibn Ḍubayʿa ibn Qays ibn Thaʿlaba, grandfather of the poet Ṭarafa ibn al-ʿAbd, and after it:
والحرب لا يبقى لجا ... حمها التخيل والمراح
إلا الفتى الصبار في النّ ... نجدات والفرس الوقاح
والنثرة الحصداء وال ... ... بيض المكلّل والرماح
وتساقط الأوشاظ والذّ ... نبات إذ جهد الفضاح والكر بعد الفر إذ ... كره التقدم وال
نطاح كشفت لهم عن ساقها ... وبدا من الشر الصراح
(In war, swagger and high spirits do not endure its blaze — only the young man patient in hardships and the hardy horse, the tightly-woven coat of mail, the crowned helmets and the spears; the hangers-on and the tail-ends fall away when disgrace presses hard, and there is wheeling back after flight when advancing and butting are loathed. It bared its shin to them, and sheer evil appeared.)
The word āyīn in the poetry of Abū Nuwās:
In the I'rab section there occurred the saying of Alexander, in which he says: "Stealing victory is not of the āyīn of kings." We would like to cite some verses of Abū Nuwās in which he used the word āyīn, and it came out light and graceful despite its strangeness. Abū Nuwās said, describing what happened to him at the monastery of Nahrādhān:
بدير نهراذان لي مجلس ... وملعب وسط بساتينه
رحت إليه ومعي قينة ... نزوره يوم سعانينه
بكلّ طلاب الهوى فاتك ... قد آثر الدنيا على دينه
حتى توافينا إلى مجلس ... تضحك ألوان رياحينه
والنرجس الغض لدى ورده ... والورد قد خفّ بنسرينه
وجيء بالدن على مرفع ... وخاتم العلج على طينه
وطاف بالكأس لنا شادن ... يدميه مس الكف من لينه
يكاد من اشراق خديه أن ... يختطف الابصار من دونه
فلم يزل يسقي ونلهو به ... ونأخذ القصف بآيينه حتى غدا السكران من سكره ... كالميت في بعض أحايينه
(At the monastery of Nahrādhān I have a sitting-place and a playground amid its gardens. I went to it with a singing-girl, visiting it on its Palm Sunday, with every reckless seeker of passion who has preferred this world to his religion, until we gathered at a sitting-place where the colours of its sweet herbs laugh, the fresh narcissus beside its roses, and the roses set off by their eglantine. The wine-jar was brought on a stand, the foreigner's seal upon its clay, and a fawn-like youth went round with the cup for us, whom the touch of a hand would make bleed for his softness; from the radiance of his cheeks he almost snatches away the sight of those before him. He kept pouring, and we kept amusing ourselves with him, taking our revelry according to its āyīn, until the drunkard from his drunkenness became at times like a dead man.)
So his words «نأخذ القصف بآيينه» mean: according to its customs, its rules and its conditions.

dervis-irab:54-58.t:
* I'rab:
(وَلُوطاً إِذْ قالَ لِقَوْمِهِ أَتَأْتُونَ الْفاحِشَةَ وَأَنْتُمْ تُبْصِرُونَ): the wāw is resumptive, and the speech is resumptive, introduced to mention the fifth and last of the stories of the sūra. (لوطا) is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object) of an omitted verb, its implied form being "remember" or "We sent". If you make it "remember", (إذ) is an adverb of past time attached to "remember"; and if you make it "We sent", (إذ) is a badal ishtimāl (substitute of inclusion) of (لوطا). The clause (قال) is in the genitive by the annexation of the adverb to it; (لقومه) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (قال). The hamza is for disapproving, rebuking interrogation; (تأتون) is an imperfect verb, the wāw is the fāʿil (agent) and (الفاحشة) is the direct object, and the clause is the object of saying (maqūl al-qawl). In (وأنتم) the wāw is circumstantial and (أنتم) is a mubtadaʾ (subject); the clause (تبصرون) is the khabar (predicate) of (أنتم). What is meant is the sight of the heart, i.e. you know that it is an abomination and yet you do it. (أَإِنَّكُمْ لَتَأْتُونَ الرِّجالَ شَهْوَةً مِنْ دُونِ النِّساءِ): the hamza is for disapproving, rebuking interrogation; the rebuke was repeated to add to the condemnation and declaring loathsome this hideous deed that contravenes the laws of nature. A discussion of these deviant sexual inclinations, the depth of whose ugliness cannot be reached, will come in the Benefits section. (إن) and its noun; the lām is the shifted lām (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa), and the clause (تأتون الرجال) is its khabar; (شهوة) is a mafʿūl li-ajlihi (object of purpose) or a ḥāl (circumstantial) of the agent or the object; (من دون النساء) is attached to an omitted ḥāl of the agent. (بَلْ أَنْتُمْ قَوْمٌ تَجْهَلُونَ): (بل) is a particle of digression (iḍrāb); (أنتم) is a mubtadaʾ and (قوم) the khabar; (تجهلون) is an adjective of (قوم). (فَما كانَ جَوابَ قَوْمِهِ إِلَّا أَنْ قالُوا أَخْرِجُوا آلَ لُوطٍ مِنْ قَرْيَتِكُمْ إِنَّهُمْ أُناسٌ يَتَطَهَّرُونَ): the fāʾ is a conjunction; (ما) is negative; (كان) is an incomplete past verb; (جواب قومه) is the fronted khabar of (كان); (إلا) is a particle of restriction; (أن قالوا) is an interpreted maṣdar in the place of the nominative, the postponed noun of (كان). The clause (أخرجوا) is the object of saying; it is an imperative verb and its agent; (آل لوط) is the direct object; (من قريتكم) is attached to (أخرجوا). (إنهم) gives the reason for expelling them; (إن) and its noun, and (أناس) is its khabar, and the clause (يتطهرون) is an adjective, i.e. they keep themselves clean of this filthy act. (فَأَنْجَيْناهُ وَأَهْلَهُ إِلَّا امْرَأَتَهُ قَدَّرْناها مِنَ الْغابِرِينَ): the fāʾ conjoins to an omitted, supplied element understood from the context, i.e. so Lot went out with his family from their land after he sensed their scheming, their plotting and their awaiting misfortunes for him. (أنجيناه) is a past verb, an agent and a direct object; (أهله) is conjoined to the hāʾ, or a mafʿūl maʿahu (object of accompaniment); (إلا) is a particle of exception and (امرأته) is the excepted; the clause (قدرناها) is a ḥāl; (قدرناها) is a past verb, an agent and a direct object; (من الغابرين) is attached to (قدرناها), i.e. those who remained in the punishment. (وَأَمْطَرْنا عَلَيْهِمْ مَطَراً فَساءَ مَطَرُ الْمُنْذَرِينَ): the wāw is a conjunction; (أمطرنا) is a verb and its agent; (عليهم) is attached to (أمطرنا); (مطرا) is a direct object. In (فساء) the fāʾ is a conjunction and (ساء) is a past verb of blame, and (مطر المنذرين) is the agent.

* Benefits:
Narcissism and sexual deviance:
Modern philosophers trace the phenomena of deviance in the sexual instincts back to narcissism; therefore we must explain this narcissism as the psychoanalysts understand it.
The ancient Greeks gave the name Narcissus to a youth of legend, of surpassing beauty and bewitching charms, who captivated whoever saw him and, with his beauty and his vanity, brought misery to the hearts of bashful virgins; yet he paid them no heed and did not respond to their supplication. He continued thus until heaven resounded with the prayers of his lovers and their entreaties to the gods to turn them away from him or turn him away from them. Nemesis, goddess of retribution and requital, answered this prayer and decreed that he should be madly in love with himself and should meet from himself the misery that his lovers met from him. The tellers of the legends said: no sooner had he gone to drink from a clear spring than he glimpsed his image in its water, and stopped at it marvelling at its beauty; the enchantment distracted him from his affairs, and he did not leave his place, bent over the water to gaze his fill on that image and slake his thirst by looking at it; but looking only increased his longing and yearning, and longing only increased his emaciation and withering, until he perished. The water-nymphs went to look for his remains and found in his place nothing but a drooping narcissus gazing at the water, never raising its sight to the sky. So the narcissus is forever drooping, its eye open, never sated with looking at its reflection on the banks of streams and pools. There are other versions of this legend, depicting the echo, wariness and torpor, which do not depart from this gist and attach to the instincts or inclinations and sensations which the malady of narcissism comprises. For that reason the psychoanalysts chose it, and found no term more suitable for the symptoms of that psychological phenomenon, together with the term's ancient roots in the Greek language, which they choose for coining new names in the sciences. The first to introduce this term into psychological medicine was Dr. Havelock Ellis, the famous pioneer of sexual research; then the psychiatrists broadened the study of this malady, traced its symptoms and concomitants, and investigated which are its primary concomitants and which its secondary or derivative ones. Of its branches that relate to the study of deviants, two concern us here:
1- One of them is called auto-eroticism (self-desire).
2- The second of them is called self-idolisation.
Auto-eroticism predominates in physical cases accompanied by disorder of the sexual functions in the person concerned, and the disorder of these functions reaches the point that the afflicted person ejaculates if he looks long at his body naked in the mirror and the like, and that he desires his body as though it were the body of a person foreign to him; but it is a desire which the patient exaggerates.
Self-idolisation predominates in emotional and intellectual cases: the afflicted person takes himself as an idol which he worships, holds dear and pampers. So the concomitant of disguise and personification is indispensable in sexual deviance, which is a person's passionate love for himself from the side of lust. The deviant in loving his own sex or loving the other sex finds what he seeks and fulfils his aim; but the one who desires his own body is not able to fulfil his aim from it without contriving that by disguise and personification: he clothes his personality as another person whom he imagines to be himself or to take the place of himself, as the masturbator does when he puts a picture before himself.
Furthermore, it is useful for whoever longs to know the development of theories on sexual questions to refer to the books written on this subject; they shed light on the problem but do not solve it, because none of them has come to downplay the differences between the two sexes, nor to the claim of those who claim that the human being is bisexual, a mixture of masculinity and femininity by nature, and that sexual deviance in him is a general innate disposition that takes on its phases according to age from childhood to full growth in both sexes, as Freud and his followers say.
Abū Nuwās, who was one of the leading figures of the narcissists, depicted these phases in the best manner, as he frequented the places of study after this fashion according to his custom, in his words:
إذا ما وطئ الأمر ... د للعلم حصى المسجد
فقل حلّ لنا عقدا ... من الفقه واستفسد
فإن كان عروضيا ... فقولوا سجد الهدهد
وإن أعجبه النحو ... فها ذاك له أجود
وإن مال إلى الفقه ... فللفقه له أفسد
وان كان كلاميا ... فحرّك طرف المقود
وميله إلى الخير ... فقيه قرب ما يبعد وخذه كيفما شئت- اقتضابا أو على موعد وقل: هذا قضاء الله هل يدفع أو يجحد
(When a beardless youth treads the pebbles of the mosque in search of knowledge, say: "Untie for us a knot of jurisprudence", and seek to corrupt him. If he is a prosodist, say: "The hoopoe prostrated"; if grammar pleases him, that is better for him; if he inclines to jurisprudence, then jurisprudence is more corrupting for him; if he is a theologian, then tug the end of the halter; and incline him towards good, for in it is the nearness of what is far. Take him however you wish, on the spur of the moment or by appointment, and say: "This is Allah's decree — can it be repelled or denied?")
And he ended, speaking plainly:
فيا من وطئ المسجد ... من ذي بهجة أغيد
أنا قست على نفسي ... فهذا الأمر لا أجحد
(O you of radiant, supple youth who tread the mosque: I have judged by myself, and this matter I do not deny.)
We end this discussion; it was something necessary, even if this is not its place.
Correcting the transmission of a verse of Abū Nuwās in al-Kashshāf:
Al-Zamakhsharī mentioned in his Kashshāf, in the course of speaking about the people of Lot; he said:
«… They used to commit it in their assembly openly, not concealing themselves from one another, out of dissoluteness, shamelessness and immersion in sin; and it is as if Abū Nuwās built on their way his saying:
وبح باسم ما تأتي وذرني من الكنى ... فلا خير في اللذات من دونها ستر
(Openly name what you do, and leave me be of allusions; there is no good in pleasures behind a veil.)»
The correct transmission is «وبح باسم من تهوى ودعني من الكنى» ("Openly name the one you love, and spare me allusions") — the verse; and it is from a splendid ode whose beginning is:
ألا فاسقني خمرا وقل لي هي الخمر ... ولا تسقني سرا إذا أمكن الجهر
(Come, give me wine to drink and tell me "It is wine"; and do not give me to drink in secret when openness is possible.)
And after the verse:
فعيش الفتى في سكرة بعد سكرة ... فإن طال هذا عنده قصر العمر
(The young man's life is in one drunkenness after another; if this lasts long for him, life is shortened.)
And after it:
وما الغرم إلا أن تراني صاحيا ... وما الغرم إلا أن يتعتعني السكر
(The only loss is that you see me sober; the only gain [Translator's note: the source repeats «الغرم», "loss", in both hemistichs; the commonly transmitted second half reads «الغُنْم», "gain"] is that drunkenness makes me stagger.)
We do not pass you by without pausing at the first verse, for he said «وقل لي هي الخمر» ("and tell me: it is wine"). This may seem padding at first glance, but if the reader remembers that the human being has five senses, he will know that Abū Nuwās intended to bring in the sense of hearing, which remains deprived of the pleasure of wine while drinking it; so he asked his drinking-companion to address him with its name so as to include his sense of hearing. This is among the marvels of his acuteness.

dervis-irab:1-6.t:
* I'rab:
(طس. تِلْكَ آياتُ الْقُرْآنِ وَكِتابٍ مُبِينٍ): the discussion of the i'rab and meaning of «طس» has preceded in the treatment of the opening letters of the sūras. «تلك» is a mubtadaʾ (subject) and «آيات القرآن» its khabar (predicate); «كتاب مبين» is conjoined to «القرآن», and «مبين» is an adjective. The secret of the indefiniteness and the conjunction will come in the Rhetoric section.
(هُدىً وَبُشْرى لِلْمُؤْمِنِينَ): «هدى» may be accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial), the governing word being the demonstrative sense contained in «تلك», i.e., guiding [Translator's note: the source prints «هاديه», evidently for «هادية»] and giving glad tidings; and it may be nominative as the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e., "it is guidance and glad tidings". The meaning of its being guidance for the believers, when they are already guided, is its increasing them in their guidance.
(الَّذِينَ يُقِيمُونَ الصَّلاةَ وَيُؤْتُونَ الزَّكاةَ وَهُمْ بِالْآخِرَةِ هُمْ يُوقِنُونَ): «الذين» is a naʿt (adjective) of «المؤمنين», and you may cut it off (qaṭʿ) as the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e., "they are those who". The clause «يقيمون الصلاة» is the ṣila (relative clause) of «الذين», and the clause «يؤتون الزكاة» is conjoined to «يقيمون الصلاة». «وهم»: the wāw is of ḥāl, and «هم» is a mubtadaʾ, or the wāw is a conjunction; the clause «يوقنون» is its khabar. «بالآخرة» are attached to (mutaʿalliq) «يوقنون». The (second) «هم» is a mubtadaʾ brought in to separate between the mubtadaʾ and its khabar [Translator's note: so in the source; the sense is that it was repeated because «بالآخرة» separated the first «هم» from its khabar], so that it adjoins the khabar in form. The secret of the change in the arrangement will come in the Rhetoric section.
(إِنَّ الَّذِينَ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالْآخِرَةِ زَيَّنَّا لَهُمْ أَعْمالَهُمْ فَهُمْ يَعْمَهُونَ): resumptive speech, brought to explain the reason for their unbelief and their bewilderment and wavering in their deeds. «إن» and its noun; the clause «لا يؤمنون» is the ṣila of «الذين»; «بالآخرة» is a preposition and its genitive noun, attached to «يؤمنون»; the clause «زينا» is the khabar of «إن». «زينا» is a verb and its fāʿil (agent); «لهم» are attached to «زينا»; «أعمالهم» is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object). The fāʾ is a conjunction; «هم» is a mubtadaʾ and the clause «يعمهون» its khabar, i.e., they are bewildered and waver between abandoning them, because they are clearly false and manifestly evil, and continuing in them. It has also been said that «يعمهون» means they continue without wavering, since the thought of giving them up never crossed their minds for a moment; this is fine and strong, but ʿamah, as al-Zamakhsharī and other authorities on the language say, is wavering and bewilderment, like the state of one who has lost the road. It is related of a certain Bedouin that he entered the market, never having seen it before, and said: "I saw the people ʿamihīn," meaning wavering in their activities and occupations. The lexicons almost agree that «العمه» is the maṣdar (verbal noun) of «عمه يعمه» and «يعمه», of the patterns of ḍaraba and fataḥa: ʿamahan, ʿumūhan, ʿumūhiyyatan and ʿamahānan, i.e., he was bewildered in his way or his affair and wavered in error; so he is ʿamih, plural ʿamihūn, and ʿāmih, plural ʿāmihūn and ʿummah.
(أُوْلئِكَ الَّذِينَ لَهُمْ سُوءُ الْعَذابِ وَهُمْ فِي الْآخِرَةِ هُمُ الْأَخْسَرُونَ): «أولئك» is a mubtadaʾ and «الذين» its khabar; «لهم» is a fronted khabar and «سوء العذاب» a postponed mubtadaʾ, and the clause is the ṣila. «هم» is a mubtadaʾ; «في الآخرة» are attached to «الأخسرون», and «الأخسرون» is its khabar; «هم» is a mubtadaʾ brought in to separate between the mubtadaʾ and its khabar so that it adjoins the khabar in form; its discussion has preceded. It must also be pointed out that His word «الأخسرون» may be in its proper sense of preference (tafḍīl), relative to the disbelievers, or it may be for intensification, not for sharing, because the believer has no loss at all in the Hereafter.
(وَإِنَّكَ لَتُلَقَّى الْقُرْآنَ مِنْ لَدُنْ حَكِيمٍ عَلِيمٍ): the wāw is resumptive; «إن» and its noun, the shifted lām (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa), and the clause «تلقى» is its khabar. The nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent) is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "anta" (you), and «القرآن» is a second direct object. «من لدن» — the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to «تلقى»; «حكيم» is muḍāf ilayhi and «عليم» an adjective.

* Rhetoric:
1- Indefiniteness:
As for indefiniteness: «الكتاب المبين» was made indefinite so as to be rendered vague by the indefiniteness and thereby more majestic; similar to it is «مقعد صدق عند مليك مقتدر». As for its being conjoined to «القرآن» although it is the Qur'an itself, that is of the kind of conjoining one of two attributes to the other, as when you say: "This is the deed of the generous one and the bountiful, noble one"; and also because the conjoined term contains an attribute additional to the concept of the term it is conjoined to.
2- Repetition of the pronoun:
In His words «وهم بالآخرة هم يوقنون» the pronoun was repeated, so that the meaning of the speech became: none is certain of the Hereafter with true certainty except these who combine faith and righteous action, because fear of the Hereafter makes them bear hardships. We have mentioned before that placing the pronoun as a mubtadaʾ gives restriction (ḥaṣr), as in the words of the Exalted «هم ينشرون», whose meaning is "none raises the dead but they". As for the reason for its repetition here, it is that the original speech was «هم يوقنون بالآخرة»; then the genitive was placed before its governing word out of concern for it, and it came to separate the mubtadaʾ and the khabar. It was desired that the khabar follow directly on the mubtadaʾ, but the genitive had come between them, so its mention was refreshed (ṭurriya) so that the khabar would follow it [Translator's note: the source prints «فطري ذكره ليلية الخبر»; «ليليه» seems intended]; and the purpose of concern for the preposition and its genitive noun was not lost, since it remained fronted as it was. It is not objectionable for a word to be repeated, separated for its sake alone, after something that calls for refreshing it.
3- Expression by the nominal and the verbal clause:
We have said in places in this book that expression is sometimes by the nominal clause and sometimes by the verbal clause, and that this is not left to arbitrariness; one of the two expressions is chosen over the other for a kind of emphasis, intensification, continuity or discontinuity. Faith and certainty in the Hereafter are a fixed matter whose permanence is required, so He brought it as a nominal clause and made its khabar an imperfect verb, saying «وهم بالآخرة هم يوقنون», to indicate that their certainty continues by way of constant renewal. As for performing the prayer and giving the zakāt, they are among the things that recur and are renewed at their appointed times, so He brought them as two verbs, saying «الذين يقيمون الصلاة ويؤتون الزكاة».

* Benefits:
Imam al-Zamakhsharī raised a question on this matter based on his Muʿtazilite principle: «If you say: how did He attribute the adorning of their deeds to Himself, when He attributed it to Satan in His words "And Satan adorned for them their deeds"?» And he answered: «I say: between the two attributions there is a difference, namely that attributing it to Satan is literal (ḥaqīqa) and attributing it to Allah the Mighty and Majestic is figurative (majāz). It has two routes in the science of bayān. The first is that it be of the figurative usage called istiʿāra (metaphor); the second is that it be of the majāz ḥukmī (figurative attribution). The first route: when He gave them enjoyment through long life and ample provision, and they made Allah's favour to them in that and His beneficence toward them a means to following their lusts, their insolence, their preferring ease and luxury, and their aversion to the difficult obligations and wearisome hardships incumbent on them, it was as if He had adorned their deeds for them by that. The angels, Allah's blessings be upon them, alluded to this in His words "But You gave them and their fathers enjoyment until they forgot the remembrance." The second route: His giving Satan respite and leaving him free to adorn for them is an evident connection (mulābasa) with the adorning, so it was attributed to Him, because figurative attribution is validated by some connection. It has also been said that they are the good deeds which they were obliged to do: Allah adorned them for them, but they were blind to them and went astray; this is ascribed to al-Ḥasan.» [Translator's note: the source does not mark clearly where al-Zamakhsharī's quotation ends; it is closed here.]
The people of the Sunna answered that this answer is built on the corrupt principle of the obligation to observe what is good and best (al-ṣalāḥ wa-l-aṣlaḥ) and the impossibility of Allah the Exalted creating for the servant anything but what is in his interest; hence he made the adorning by Allah the Exalted figurative and by Satan literal. Had he reversed the answer, he would have attained what is right. Consider his inclination to the other interpretation — that the deeds of righteousness are meant — despite its remoteness, because it does not expose his principle to refutation. Moreover, adorning does occur concerning good, in the words of the Exalted «ولكن الله حبب إليكم الإيمان وزينه في قلوبكم», though most of its occurrences concern what is not righteousness, as in His words «زين للناس حب الشهوات», «زين للذين كفروا الحياة الدنيا» and «كذلك زين للمسرفين». What makes it unlikely that it be taken as deeds of righteousness is the annexation of the deeds to them in His word «أعمالهم»; deeds of righteousness are not annexed to them, because they never did them, and the apparent sense of the annexation gives that. Do you not see the words of the Exalted «ولما يدخل الإيمان في قلوبكم» and His words «قل لا تمنوا علي إسلامكم بل الله يمن عليكم أن هداكم للإيمان»? He left faith in both places unannexed to them, because it did not proceed from them, and annexed outward Islam to them, because it proceeded from them.

dervis-irab:59-64.t:
* Vocabulary:
(حَدائِقَ): plural of ḥadīqa, i.e. a garden, from aḥdaqa bil-shayʾ, "it surrounded the thing". Since the garden is surrounded by walls it was called ḥadīqa; otherwise it is not called by that name. In al-Miṣbāḥ: «Al-ḥadīqa is a garden with a wall around it, faʿīla in the sense of mafʿūla, because the wall surrounds it (aḥdaqa bihā), i.e. encloses it; then they extended it until they applied ḥadīqa to a garden even without a wall; the plural is ḥadāʾiq.» In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: «Al-ḥadīqa: every garden with a wall around it.» Among their sayings: «Your letter reached me, and I took my pleasure in the most delightful of its meadows and the splendour of its gardens.»

* I'rab:
(قُلِ الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ وَسَلامٌ عَلى عِبادِهِ الَّذِينَ اصْطَفى): resumptive speech, introduced to command His Messenger ﷺ to praise Him, the Exalted, and to send peace upon the chosen, the excellent ones of His creation. It is as if this praise were an elegant opening (barāʿat istihlāl) for the proofs and evidences He will present of the divine unity, knowledge and power, whose mention will come; and that is after He finished the stories of these five sūras [Translator's note: so in the source, «السور الخمس»; the context indicates the five stories of this sūra]. (قل) is an imperative verb whose fāʿil (agent) is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "you", i.e. O Muḥammad, so that it may be a model which every writer and orator follows and on whose pattern one proceeds in every beneficial science. (الحمد) is a mubtadaʾ (subject) and (لله) its khabar (predicate); (سلام) is a mubtadaʾ, what permitted beginning with it [as an indefinite] being the meaning of supplication in it; (على عباده) is the khabar; (الذين) is an adjective of (عباده), and the clause (اصطفى) is the ṣila (relative clause), the referring pronoun being omitted, i.e. "He chose them"; they are the believers qualified for this world and the Hereafter. (آللَّهُ خَيْرٌ أَمَّا يُشْرِكُونَ): the hamza is for interrogation; (الله) is a mubtadaʾ and (خير) the khabar; (أم) is a conjunction; (ما) is a relative noun applying to their gods, and the clause (يشركون) is the ṣila. (أَمَّنْ خَلَقَ السَّماواتِ وَالْأَرْضَ وَأَنْزَلَ لَكُمْ مِنَ السَّماءِ ماءً فَأَنْبَتْنا بِهِ حَدائِقَ ذاتَ بَهْجَةٍ): (أم) is disconnected (munqaṭiʿa), because its condition is lacking, namely the precedence of the interrogative hamza; it means (بل), and the digression is in the sense of silencing and rebuking. (من) is a mubtadaʾ and the clause (خلق السموات والأرض) is the ṣila; the khabar of (من) is omitted, its implied form being "better, or what they associate?", so what was stated in the first interrogation is supplied, relying on it. This is what al-Zamakhsharī chose, and it is fine and consistent with the speech. Abū al-Faḍl al-Rāzī said:
«A balancing clause must be implied, and that implied clause has become like what is uttered because the import indicates it. The implied form of that clause is: "Is He who created the heavens and the earth like him who did not create?", and likewise its sisters. What was implied in these places has been made explicit elsewhere, as in the saying of the Exalted: أفمن يخلق كمن لا يخلق.»
We see no clear difference between the two views. (أنزل) is conjoined to (خلق); (لكم) is a ḥāl (circumstantial); (من السماء) is attached to (أنزل); (ماء) is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object). The fāʾ is a conjunction, and (أنبتنا) is conjoined to what precedes by way of iltifāt (shift of person), which will come in the Rhetoric section; (به) is attached to (أنبتنا); (حدائق) is the direct object and (ذات بهجة) is an adjective of (حدائق); what permitted its being singular is that the qualified noun is a plural of abundance for non-rational things.
(ما كانَ لَكُمْ أَنْ تُنْبِتُوا شَجَرَها): the clause is a second naʿt (adjective) of (حدائق), or a ḥāl of it because it is specified by the adjective. (ما) is negative; (كان) is an incomplete past verb; (لكم) is the fronted khabar of (كان), and (أن) and what falls in its domain is its postponed noun; (تنبتوا) is an imperfect verb in the accusative by (أن), the wāw is the agent and (شجرها) is the object. (أَإِلهٌ مَعَ اللَّهِ بَلْ هُمْ قَوْمٌ يَعْدِلُونَ): the hamza is for disapproving interrogation containing the meaning of negation; (إله) is a mubtadaʾ, beginning with it being permitted because it conveys information on account of the interrogation; (مع الله) is an adverb attached to an omitted khabar. (بل) is a particle of digression (iḍrāb) whose meaning is silencing; this expression is repeated five times, as you will see. (هم) is a mubtadaʾ and (قوم) the khabar, and the clause (يعدلون) is an adjective. (أَمَّنْ جَعَلَ الْأَرْضَ قَراراً وَجَعَلَ خِلالَها أَنْهاراً): the parsing of this construction has preceded, so draw the analogy with it. (قرارا) is the second object of (جعل); (وجعل خلالها أنهارا) is conjoined to the first clause. (خلالها) may be an adverb of (جعل) in the sense of "created", transitive to one object, or in the position of the second object, taking it in the sense of "made into"; on the first view (قرارا) is a ḥāl. [Translator's note: so in the source; on the first view it is presumably (أنهارا) in the second clause that would be the single object.] (وَجَعَلَ لَها رَواسِيَ): a conjoined clause. (وَجَعَلَ بَيْنَ الْبَحْرَيْنِ حاجِزاً أَإِلهٌ مَعَ اللَّهِ بَلْ أَكْثَرُهُمْ لا يَعْلَمُونَ): the clause is conjoined to what precedes, and its parsing has preceded.
(أَمَّنْ يُجِيبُ الْمُضْطَرَّ إِذا دَعاهُ وَيَكْشِفُ السُّوءَ): its parsing has preceded; the clause (دعاه) is in the position of the genitive by the annexation of the adverb to it; (المضطر) is a passive participle, and its ṭāʾ was originally the tāʾ of the iftiʿāl form. (وَيَجْعَلُكُمْ خُلَفاءَ الْأَرْضِ أَإِلهٌ مَعَ اللَّهِ قَلِيلًا ما تَذَكَّرُونَ): its parsing has preceded. (قليلا) is an adjective of an omitted maṣdar (verbal noun) or of an omitted time; (ما) is redundant (zāʾida), to make the little less; (تذكرون) is an imperfect verb one of whose two tāʾs has been dropped, and the wāw is the agent. (أَمَّنْ يَهْدِيكُمْ فِي ظُلُماتِ الْبَرِّ وَالْبَحْرِ): its parsing has preceded. (وَمَنْ يُرْسِلُ الرِّياحَ بُشْراً بَيْنَ يَدَيْ رَحْمَتِهِ أَإِلهٌ مَعَ اللَّهِ تَعالَى اللَّهُ عَمَّا يُشْرِكُونَ): its parsing has also preceded. (أَمَّنْ يَبْدَؤُا الْخَلْقَ ثُمَّ يُعِيدُهُ وَمَنْ يَرْزُقُكُمْ مِنَ السَّماءِ وَالْأَرْضِ): its parsing has also preceded. (أَإِلهٌ مَعَ اللَّهِ قُلْ هاتُوا بُرْهانَكُمْ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ صادِقِينَ): (إن) is conditional and its apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ) is omitted, its implied form being "then bring your proof". We have stated before that His saying «أإله» is mentioned five times: the first ends with His saying «بل هم يعدلون», the second with His saying «بل أكثرهم لا يعلمون», the third with His saying «قليلا ما يذكرون», the fourth with His saying «تعالى الله عما يشركون», and the fifth with His saying «قل هاتوا برهانكم إن كنتم صادقين». [Translator's note: the source quotes the first as «بل هم يعدلون» and the third as «قليلا ما يذكرون»; the verses read «بَلْ هُمْ قَوْمٌ يَعْدِلُونَ» and «قَلِيلًا ما تَذَكَّرُونَ».]

* Rhetoric:
Iltifāt (shift of person) in His words «فأنبتنا به حدائق ذات بهجة» after His words «أم من خلق السموات والأرض وأنزل لكم من السماء ماء»: in conveying the report He moved from the third person to the first person, speaking of Himself, in His words «فأنبتنا». The secret in it is to emphasise that the act of causing to grow belongs exclusively to Him, the Exalted, and to announce that causing the gardens of various kinds to grow, with what appears in them of embellishments of colours and beauties of forms, diverse tastes and different scents varying in the sweetness of their fragrance and perfume — all of that none is able to do except a powerful Creator, and He is Allah alone. Therefore He reinforced this exclusiveness by saying after that «ما كان لكم أن تنبتوا شجرها». Abū Nuwās grasped this truth and said:
تأمل في رياض الأرض وانظر ... إلى آثار ما صنع المليك
عيون من لجين شاخصات ... بأنظار هي الذهب السبيك
على قضب الزبرجد شاهدات ... بأن الله ليس له شريك
(Contemplate the meadows of the earth and look at the traces of what the Sovereign has made: eyes of silver, gazing with pupils that are molten gold, upon stems of chrysolite, bearing witness that Allah has no partner.)
Did Abū Nuwās repent?
Furthermore, perhaps you wonder at these verses brimming with deep faith and issuing from a man like Abū Nuwās. Those who accused him did not wrong him, nor did they lack proofs for accusing him of corruption; but they wronged philosophy, thinking it a path leading those acquainted with it to heresy (zandaqa) and its doctrines. There is no heresy here with Abū Nuwās, and no doctrine other than licentiousness and love of showing off. Ibrāhīm al-Naẓẓām was among the most learned of the people of his time in what they call the sciences of the ancients, and Abū Nuwās used to attend his lessons; he would forbid him from vulgarity and remind him of the threat [of punishment], saying to him: "Whoever looks forward to Allah's promise must beware of His threat." But he would not desist from his idle talk and licentiousness, until he despaired of him and expelled him from his circle. So he composed about him his ode which became famous as al-Ibrāhīmiyya, whose opening is famous and widely circulated:
دع عنك لومي فإن اللوم إغراء ... وداوني بالتي كانت هي الداء
(Leave off blaming me, for blame is an incitement, and cure me with that which was itself the disease.)
And in it he mocks al-Naẓẓām:
فقل لمن يدعي في العلم فلسفة ... حفظت شيئا وغابت عنك أشياء
لا تخطر العفو إن كنت امرأ حرجا ... فإن خطرك بالدين إزراء
(Say to him who claims philosophy in knowledge: you have memorised something and many things have escaped you. Do not bar pardon if you are a scrupulous man, for your barring it is a disparagement of religion.)
Abū Nuwās was nothing but a reckless libertine, and licentiousness in the custom of his milieu was wit. The emir Abū al-ʿAbbās Muḥammad advised him to repent of licentiousness, and he said to him: "As for licentiousness, not everyone is able to be licentious; licentiousness is only wit, and in it I do not go beyond the bounds of good manners or exceed its measure. As for sins, in them I trust in the pardon of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and the saying of the Exalted: «يا عبادي الذين أسرفوا على أنفسهم لا تقنطوا من رحمة الله إن الله يغفر الذنوب جميعا»." Abū Nuwās picked up the errors of the Murjiʾa and their saying: «With faith, no sin at all, great or small, does harm; and with polytheism, no good deed at all is of benefit». He proclaimed that, and it appears that it beguiled him:
ترى عندنا ما يسخط الله كله ... من العمل المردي الفتى ما خلا الشركا
(You see with us all that angers Allah of the deeds that ruin a young man — except polytheism.)
Then he modified his theory somewhat and was content to say that grave sins do not place their doer among the unbelievers nor deprive him of hope in Allah's pardon; his saying on that is famous:
تكثر ما استطعت من الخطايا ... فإنك بالغ ربا غفورا
تعض ندامة كفيك مما ... تركت مخافة النار السرورا
