(وكل): the wāw is circumstantial or a conjunction; (كل) is a mubtadaʾ, beginning with it being permitted because of the meaning of generality in it and because its tanwīn is a substitute for the muḍāf ilayhi, i.e. "and all of them, after their being brought to life on the Day of Resurrection". The clause (أتوه) is the khabar; the future is expressed with the past because its occurrence is certain, as though it had actually occurred. (داخرين) is a ḥāl.
(وَتَرَى الْجِبالَ تَحْسَبُها جامِدَةً وَهِيَ تَمُرُّ مَرَّ السَّحابِ): the wāw is a conjunction; (ترى الجبال) is an imperfect verb in the nominative, a latent agent whose implied form is "you", and a direct object; the seeing is visual. The clause (تحسبها) is a ḥāl of (الجبال); the hāʾ is the first object of (تحسبها) and (جامدة) its second object. In (وهي) the wāw is circumstantial and (هي) is a mubtadaʾ, the clause (تمر) is the khabar, and the clause is a ḥāl of (جامدة). [Translator's note: the source does not parse (مر السحاب), a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object) and muḍāf ilayhi.] (صُنْعَ اللَّهِ الَّذِي أَتْقَنَ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ إِنَّهُ خَبِيرٌ بِما تَفْعَلُونَ): (صنع) is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object) emphasising the content of the clause before it, the maṣdar (verbal noun) being annexed to its agent; (الذي) is an adjective of (الله), and the clause (أتقن) is the ṣila; (كل شيء) is the object of (أتقن). (إن), its noun and its khabar; (بما) is attached to (خبير), and the clause (تفعلون) is the ṣila of (ما).

* Rhetoric:
In these verses there are several devices, which we summarise as follows:
1- Rational metonymy (al-majāz al-ʿaqlī):
In His words «والنهار مبصرا», seeing is attributed to time, which is not rational. He did not bring the speech as a counterpart of what precedes it, namely «ألم يروا أنا جعلنا الليل ليسكنوا فيه»; rather He made one of them a reason and the other a ḥāl, because the correspondence has been observed from the side of the meaning, since the meaning of «مبصرا» is "so that they may see in it the ways of moving about and earning". This is natural, unaffected composition.
2- Reporting the future with the past:
He reported the future with the past in His words «ففزع من في السموات ومن في الأرض», whereas the context required that He also bring the future; but He turned to the past to convey the certainty of the terror and that it will come to pass without doubt, because the past verb indicates the existence of the act and its being certain.
3- Antithesis (al-ṭibāq):
In His words «وترى الجبال تحسبها جامدة وهي تمر مر السحاب» there is a marvellous antithesis between immobility and rapid motion: He made what appears to the eye of the onlooker like the mountain in its immobility and firmness, yet it is swift, passing at a rapid pace as the clouds pass. This is the way of great bodies of large number: when they move, their movement can scarcely be discerned, as al-Nābigha said, describing an army:
بأرعن مثل الطود تحسب أنهم ... وقوف لحاج والركاب تهملج
(With a towering host like a great mountain, you would think them standing still for some need, while the mounts are trotting swiftly.)
This is a splendid verse. Al-arʿan is the high mountain, and he borrowed it for the army, then likened it to al-ṭawd, which is the huge mountain, to convey exaggeration in great number. Al-ḥāj is a collective noun whose singular is ḥāja; al-rikāb are the riding beasts, having no singular from its own root; al-hamlaja is a smooth, swift gait, an Arabicised Persian word. In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: «The himlāj, among the pack-horses — its plural is hamālīj — and its gait is hamlaja; Arabicised Persian.» He says: we fought the enemy with a mighty army; you would think them standing still for some need because of their great number, while their mounts are hastening on.
Al-Zamakhsharī has an eloquent description of these verses, which we cite as follows:
«Look at the eloquence of this speech, the beauty of its composition and arrangement, the firmness of its binding [Translator's note: the source has «إضماده»], the solidity of its explanation, and how each part takes hold of the waist-band of another, as though it were cast in a single casting. For some reason it has disabled the powers and silenced the eloquent tongues. Something like this maṣdar — i.e. «صنع الله» — when it comes after a speech, comes as a witness to its soundness and a proclaimer of its rightness, and that it could only have been as it was. Do you not see His sayings «صنع الله», «وعد الله» and «فطرة الله» — after He marked them, by annexing them to Himself, with the mark of magnification — how He followed them with His sayings «الذي أتقن كل شيء», «ومن أحسن من الله صبغة», «ولا يخلف الله الميعاد» and «لا تبديل لخلق الله»?»

dervis-irab:20-26.t:
* Vocabulary:
(الْهُدْهُدَ): «الهدهد» and «الهُداهد» [Translator's note: the source prints «الهدهد» twice without vowels; two vocalizations are presumably meant] is a bird with stripes and many colours; the singular is «هدهدة», «هدهدة» and «هداهدة», and the plural «هداهد» and «هداهيد». They say "more sharp-sighted than a hoopoe", because they claim that it sees water under the ground. «الهدهد» is also any bird that coos, and many pigeons. Its story with Solomon will come in the Benefits section.
(فَمَكَثَ): with ḍamma and with fatḥa on the kāf; the first is of the pattern of qaruba and the second of the pattern of naṣara. In al-Qāmūs and elsewhere: «مكث يمكث», of the pattern of naṣara: makthan, mukthan, mukūthan, makathānan, makkīthā and makkīthāʾ in a place — he stayed and remained; so he is «ماكث», and the noun is «المكث» and «المُكث». «مكُث يمكُث», of the pattern of qaruba, makātha: he stayed and was composed (grave).
(سَبَإٍ): a land situated in the south-west of the Arabian Peninsula, in Yemen, mentioned in the books of the Old Testament and in the works of the Arabs, Greeks and Romans. It possessed a great civilization, and its inhabitants traded in gold, silver and precious stones.
Al-Zamakhsharī said in al-Kashshāf: «"Saba'" was read as a triptote and as a diptote, and it has also been transmitted with sukūn on the bāʾ. From Ibn Kathīr, in one transmission, «سبا» with alif, as in their saying "they went off like the hands of Sabā (ayādī sabā)". He is Sabaʾ ibn Yashjub ibn Yaʿrub ibn Qaḥṭān. Whoever makes it the name of the tribe does not inflect it fully; whoever makes it the name of the clan or of the greatest father [Translator's note: the source prints «الأدب الأكبر», evidently for «الأب الأكبر»] inflects it fully. The poet said:
من سبأ الحاضرين مأرب إذ ... يبنون من دون سيله العرما
(Of Sabaʾ, the settled dwellers of Maʾrib, when they built the dam against its torrent.)
And he said:
الواردون وتيم في ذرا سبأ ... قد عض أعناقهم جلد الجواميس
(Those who come to water, and Taym, in the shelter of Sabaʾ — buffalo-hide [straps] have bitten their necks.)
Then the city of Maʾrib was called Sabaʾ — between it and Ṣanʿāʾ is a journey of three [days] — just as Maʿāfir was named after Maʿāfir ibn Udd. It may mean the city or the people.»
The meaning of "they went off like the hands of Sabā":
One says «ذهبوا أيدي سبا», and there are two usages: «أيدي سبا» and «أيادي سبا». It has two treatments: either you compound the two nouns into a single noun and make them indeclinable because they imply the conjunction, as they did with «خمسة عشر»; or, second, you annex the first to the second. Their position is accusative as a ḥāl (circumstantial), and what is meant is "they went off dispersed and scattered" and the like. If it is objected that «سبا» is definite, it is answered that compounding them dropped the sense of proper-namehood and they became one noun. The origin of this proverb is that when [the people of] Sabaʾ ibn Yashjub ibn Yaʿrub ibn Qaḥṭān were warned of the Flood of al-ʿArim, they left Yemen dispersed through the lands; so of every group that dispersed it was said: they went off like the hands of Sabā. What is meant by "hands" is the sons and the family, not the bodily limb, since the dispersal befell them; the term "hands" was borrowed because in strength and in the power to strike through them they are like hands.
(الْخَبْءَ): a maṣdar (verbal noun) in the sense of «المخبوء» (the hidden). One says «خبأت الشيء أخبؤه خبئا», of the pattern of nafaʿa, i.e., I concealed it. The khabʾ in the heavens is the rain and in the earth the plants.

* I'rab:
(وَتَفَقَّدَ الطَّيْرَ فَقالَ ما لِيَ لا أَرَى الْهُدْهُدَ أَمْ كانَ مِنَ الْغائِبِينَ): resumptive speech, to begin relating another matter that occurred to Solomon during the journey in which the story of the ants took place. «تفقد» is a past verb whose fāʿil (agent) is a latent (mustatir) pronoun, its implied form being "huwa" (he), i.e., Solomon; «الطير» is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object). «فقال» is conjoined to «تفقد». «ما» is an interrogative noun in the position of nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject), and «لي» its khabar (predicate); the clause «لا أرى الهدهد» is a ḥāl. «أم» is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿa); «كان» is an incomplete (nāqiṣ) past verb whose noun is a latent pronoun referring to the hoopoe, and «من الغائبين» is the khabar of «كان».
(لَأُعَذِّبَنَّهُ عَذاباً شَدِيداً أَوْ لَأَذْبَحَنَّهُ أَوْ لَيَأْتِيَنِّي بِسُلْطانٍ مُبِينٍ): the lām paves the way for the oath (muwaṭṭiʾa li-l-qasam); «أعذبنه» is an imperfect verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on fatḥa because of its connection with the heavy nūn of emphasis; its agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "anā" (I), and the hāʾ is the direct object. «عذابا» is a mafʿūl muṭlaq (absolute object) and «شديدا» an adjective. «أو لأذبحنه» is conjoined to «لأعذبنه», and «أو ليأتيني» is also conjoined to it; «بسلطان» are attached to (mutaʿalliq) «يأتيني», and «مبين» is an adjective.
(فَمَكَثَ غَيْرَ بَعِيدٍ فَقالَ أَحَطْتُ بِما لَمْ تُحِطْ بِهِ وَجِئْتُكَ مِنْ سَبَإٍ بِنَبَإٍ يَقِينٍ): the fāʾ is resumptive; «مكث» is a past verb with a latent agent referring to the hoopoe or to Solomon. «غير بعيد» is an adverb of time attached to «مكث», or, more correctly, an adjective of an omitted adverb whose place it has taken, i.e., "a time not far" — or "a place not far", in which case it is an adverb of place. «فقال» is conjoined to «مكث», and this supports the pronoun's referring to the hoopoe. The clause «أحطت» is the object of the saying (maqūl al-qawl); «بما» are attached to «أحطت»; the clause «لم تحط» [Translator's note: the source prints «نحط» here] is the ṣila (relative clause), and «به» are attached to «تحط». «جئتك» is conjoined to «أحطت»; «من سبأ» are attached to an omitted ḥāl, because it was originally an adjective of «نبأ»; «بنبإ» are attached to «جئتك», and «يقين» is an adjective of «نبأ».
(إِنِّي وَجَدْتُ امْرَأَةً تَمْلِكُهُمْ وَأُوتِيَتْ مِنْ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ وَلَها عَرْشٌ عَظِيمٌ): «إن» and its noun; the clause «وجدت امرأة» is the khabar of «إني»; the clause «تملكهم» is an adjective of «امرأة». «وأوتيت»: the wāw is a conjunction or of ḥāl; the clause «أوتيت» is either conjoined to the clause «تملكهم» — the conjoining of a past to an imperfect being permissible because the imperfect has the meaning of the past, i.e., "she ruled them" — or a ḥāl of the agent of «تملكهم», with «قد» implied. «من كل شيء» are attached to «أوتيت», or to an omitted word which is the second object of «أوتيت», the implied sense being likewise "of everything". «لها» is a fronted khabar, «عرش» a postponed mubtadaʾ and «عظيم» an adjective.
(وَجَدْتُها وَقَوْمَها يَسْجُدُونَ لِلشَّمْسِ مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ): the clause «وجدتها» is a badal (substitute) of «وجدت امرأة», so it falls within the scope of the khabar. «وجدتها» here takes one object, because it means "I met her"; the hāʾ is the direct object, and «قومها» is conjoined to the hāʾ or is a mafʿūl maʿahu (object of accompaniment). The clause «يسجدون» is a ḥāl of its object and what is conjoined to it; «للشمس» are attached to «يسجدون», and «من دون الله» is a ḥāl.
(وَزَيَّنَ لَهُمُ الشَّيْطانُ أَعْمالَهُمْ فَصَدَّهُمْ عَنِ السَّبِيلِ فَهُمْ لا يَهْتَدُونَ): the wāw is a conjunction; «زين» is a past verb, «لهم» are attached to it, «الشيطان» is its agent and «أعمالهم» its object. «فصدهم» is conjoined to «زين», and «عن السبيل» are attached to «صدهم». «فهم»: the fāʾ is a conjunction, «هم» a mubtadaʾ and the clause «لا يهتدون» its khabar.
(أَلَّا يَسْجُدُوا لِلَّهِ الَّذِي يُخْرِجُ الْخَبْءَ فِي السَّماواتِ وَالْأَرْضِ): the nūn must be omitted in writing, following the practice of the Muṣḥaf. «أن» is a maṣdariyya particle that makes the verb accusative, and «لا» is redundant (zāʾida); the meaning is «أن يسجدوا». This interpreted maṣdar is governed by His words «لا يهتدون», but by removal of the preposition, namely «إلى»; the meaning is "so they are not guided to prostration". On this i'rab it is not correct to pause at «يهتدون». The maṣdar may also be a badal of «أعمالهم», the implied sense being "Satan adorned for them their deeds: not prostrating"; or it may be a badal of «السبيل». It was also read with «ألا» lightened, in which case it is a particle of alerting and opening; «يا» is a vocative particle, the one addressed being omitted, and «اسجدوا» is an imperative verb. The proper spelling on this reading would have been «يا اسجدوا», but the Companions dropped the alif of «يا» and the hamzat al-waṣl of «اسجدوا» in writing, since they dropped in pronunciation, and joined «يا» to the sīn of «اسجدوا», so its form became «يسجدوا», as you see. Thus the two readings coincide in sound and script and differ in their underlying analysis. The discussion of the grammarians' disagreement over «يا» entering a verb or a particle will come in the Benefits section [Translator's note: no such discussion appears in the Benefits section of this entry]. «لله» are attached to «يسجدوا»; «الذي» is a relative, a naʿt (adjective) of «الله»; the clause «يخرج الخبء» is the ṣila; «في السموات والأرض» are attached to «الخبء», i.e., what is hidden in the heavens; or to «يخرج», «في» having the sense of «من», i.e., He brings it out from the heavens and the earth.
(وَيَعْلَمُ ما تُخْفُونَ وَما تُعْلِنُونَ): «يعلم» is conjoined to «يخرج», so it falls within the scope of the ṣila; the agent of «يعلم» is a latent pronoun referring to Allah; «ما» is a relative, the direct object; the clause «تخفون» is the ṣila, and «ما تعلنون» is conjoined to «ما تخفون».
(اللَّهُ لا إِلهَ إِلَّا هُوَ رَبُّ الْعَرْشِ الْعَظِيمِ): resumptive speech, brought to extol Allah's mighty Throne after the allusion to the throne of Bilqīs — and between the two there is a vast gulf.

* Rhetoric:
Jinās al-taṣrīf (paronomasia by variation):
In His words «وجئتك من سبأ بنبإ يقين» there is jinās al-taṣrīf, which is the difference in the form of two words by replacing one letter with another, either of the same point of articulation or of a nearby point of articulation. It is among the beauties of speech related to wording, on condition that it comes naturally, far from affectation, preserving the soundness of the meaning. Here it came adding to soundness, so it was fine and delicate. Do you not see that had He said «بخبر» instead of «بنبإ», the meaning would have been sound and straight, but it came melodious and sweet in ring because of the agreement of «سبأ» and «نبأ». Its like has preceded in His words in Sūrat al-Anʿām: «وهم ينهون عنه وينأون عنه».

* Benefits:
1- The story of Solomon and the hoopoe:
Following our custom, we give one of the reports mentioned about the story of Solomon and the hoopoe, because of the narrative roots in it and as a preparation for the gifted, inspired writers of stories:
It is related that when Solomon had finished building Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis), he prepared for the pilgrimage with his assembled host. He reached the Sanctuary and stayed there as long as he wished, and every day of his stay he offered five thousand she-camels, five thousand cows and twenty thousand sheep. Then he resolved to go to Yemen, and left Mecca in the morning heading toward Canopus (Suhayl). He reached Ṣanʿāʾ at noon and saw a beautiful land resplendent with greenery, so he alighted to take his midday meal and pray, but they did not find water. The hoopoe was his qunāqin, i.e., his guide, and it saw water under the ground as water is seen in a glass, so he looked for it for that reason. When Solomon alighted, the hoopoe soared up and saw another hoopoe perched, so it swooped down to it and described to it the kingdom of Solomon and everything that had been subjected to him. The other told it of the kingdom of Bilqīs, and that under her hand were twelve thousand commanders, and under each commander a hundred thousand, and it went with it to look, and it did not return until after the afternoon prayer. It is mentioned that a ray of sun fell on Solomon's head, so he looked, and the hoopoe's place was empty. He called the chief of the birds, the vulture, and asked him about it, but found he had no knowledge of it. Then he said to the lord of the birds, the eagle: "Bring it to me." The eagle rose into the air until it saw the world like a bowl; then it turned right and left and saw the hoopoe approaching. The eagle swooped down, making for it, and the hoopoe knew that the eagle meant it harm and said: "By the right of the One who strengthened you and gave you power, have mercy on me." So it left it and said: "Woe to you, may your mother be bereaved of you! The Prophet of Allah has sworn to punish you." It said: "And did the Prophet of Allah make no exception?" It said: "Yes, he did; he said: «or he shall bring me a clear authority»." It said: "Then I am saved." When it came near Solomon it let down its tail and wings, trailing them on the ground in humility before Solomon. When it drew close to him, he took hold of its head and pulled it toward him, and it said: "O Prophet of Allah, remember your standing before Allah." Solomon trembled and pardoned it, then asked it: "What kept you from me?" The hoopoe said: «أحطت بما لم تحط به…» to the end.
A point of eloquence:
Al-Zamakhsharī said: «If you say: he swore to one of three things; his swearing to his own two acts is unobjectionable, but how was his swearing to the hoopoe's act valid, and how did he know that it would bring an authority, so that he could say "by Allah, it shall bring me an authority"? I say: when he arranged the three with «أو» in the ruling, namely the oath, his words amounted to your saying "one of these things shall certainly happen"; that is, if the bringing of an authority occurs, there will be no punishment and no slaughter, and if not, one of these two will occur. There is no claim to knowledge in this.»
2- Who was Bilqīs?
Bilqīs was the daughter of Sharāḥīl ibn Abī Sarḥ ibn al-Ḥārith ibn Qays ibn Ṣayghī [Translator's note: so in the source; the name is usually given as Ṣayfī] ibn Sabaʾ. Ibn al-Kalbī said: her father was one of the greatest kings. Her story will come. Al-Ḥarīrī mentioned in Durrat al-Ghawwāṣ that the correct form of the word «بلقيس» is with kasra on the bāʾ, because every foreign word that is Arabized should by analogy be assimilated to the patterns of Arabic speech, and «بلقيس» is accordingly so [i.e., like «فِعليل»].
Among the reports of Sayf al-Dawla: the two Khālidīs praised him, and he sent them a page-boy and a slave-girl, each of them with a purse of money and a chest of clothes from Egypt and Syria. They wrote to him [Translator's note: the poem's lines are broken across lines in the source; they are given here as whole verses with the text unchanged]:
لم يغد شكرك في الخلائق مطلقا ... إلا ومالك في النوال حبيس
(Thanks to you have not gone forth unbounded among people except because your wealth is devoted to giving.)
خولتنا شمسا وبدرا أشرقت ... بهما لدينا الظلمة الحنديس
(You granted us a sun and a full moon, by which the pitch darkness with us has shone.)
رشنأ أتانا، وهو حسنا يوسف ... وغزالة هي بهجة، بلقيس
(A fawn came to us, in beauty a Joseph, and a gazelle who in splendour is a Bilqīs.) [Translator's note: «رشنأ» is as printed, evidently for «رشأ» (fawn).]
هذا ولم تقنع بذاك وهذه ... حتى بعثت المال وهو نفيس
(And you were not content with him and her, but sent wealth as well, and precious it is.)
أتت الوصيفة وهي تحمل بدرة ... وأتى على ظهر الوصيف الكيس
(The slave-girl came carrying a purse, and on the back of the page-boy came the bag.)
وكسوتنا مما أجادت حوكه ... مصر وزادت حسنه تنيس
(You clothed us in what Egypt wove finely and Tinnīs added to in beauty.)
فغدا لنا من جودك المأكول وال ... مشروب والمنكوح والملبوس
(So from your bounty we now have what is eaten, what is drunk, what is wed, and what is worn.)
When Sayf al-Dawla read it, he said: "They did well, except in the word «المنكوح», since it is not among the words with which kings are addressed."
The story of Bilqīs and her smooth palace was a source of inspiration for poets. Al-Buḥturī included all of it in an ode in which he praised al-Mutawakkil and mentioned the building of the famous pool; from it:
يا من رأى البركة الحسناء رؤيتها ... والآنسات إذا لاحت مغانيها
(O you who have seen the beautiful pool — the sight of it, and the fair maidens when its haunts appear,)
بحسبها أنها في فضل رتبتها ... تعدّ واحدة والبحر ثانيها
(it is enough for it that in the excellence of its rank it is counted first and the sea second to it;)
كأن جن سليمان الذين ولوا ... إبداعها فأدقوا في معانيها
(as if the jinn of Solomon had charge of creating it and made its features exquisite;)
فلو تمر بها بلقيس عن عرض ... قالت هي الصرح تمثيلا وتشبيها
(were Bilqīs to pass by it by chance, she would say: "It is the palace," by way of likeness and comparison.)
3- The prostrations of the Qur'an:
In connection with His words «ألّا يسجدوا لله»: Abū Ḥanīfa and al-Shāfiʿī agreed that the prostrations of the Qur'an are fourteen; they differed only over the prostration of «ص», which for Abū Ḥanīfa is a prostration of recitation and for al-Shāfiʿī a prostration of thanks, and over the two prostrations of Sūrat al-Ḥajj.
4- The story of the Flood of al-ʿArim and the dispersal of the Arabs "like the hands of Sabā":
We give here some of the related legends for their charm and benefit:
Sabaʾ is the father of the tribes of Yemen who were dispersed from the Dam of Maʾrib, whom Allah tore into utter pieces. He was called Sabaʾ because he was the first to take captives (sabā al-sabī). It has been said that Sabaʾ was the name of their mother and Maʾrib the name of their town. Sabaʾ was among the most beautiful of Allah's lands, the most fertile and the richest in trees and water. Allah mentioned that it was two gardens, on the right and the left. It was a month's journey by a month for the hard-riding traveller, who would travel through gardens from its beginning to its end, never facing the sun and never leaving the shade, with the water flowing, the air clear and the space wide. They remained as long as Allah willed; no king opposed them but they broke him. In early times the torrents used to overrun it, so the king of Ḥimyar gathered the people of his kingdom and consulted them about warding off the torrent. They agreed on digging channels for it to carry it to the sea. He mustered the people of his kingdom until the water was diverted, and he built a dam where the water ran down from the mountains, paving it with stones and iron, and made in it channels for the water the size of a forearm's circumference; when the torrent came, it was distributed through the channels to their gardens and crops in a measure whose benefit reached all of them. Al-Aʿshā mentioned in his poetry that Ḥimyar built it; he said:
رخام بنته لهم حمير ... إذا جاء ماؤهم لم يرم
(Marble that Ḥimyar built for them; when their water came, it did not move.)
وأروى الزروع وأعنابهم ... على سعة ماؤهم قد قسم
(It watered the crops and their vines; their water was apportioned amply.)
فعاشوا بذلك في غبطة ... فحاق بهم جارف منهدم
(So they lived thereby in happiness; then a sweeping, crashing flood overtook them.)
When the kingship came to ʿAmr ibn ʿĀmir Muzayqiyāʾ — so called because every night he tore up (yumazziq) a robe, out of pride, lest it be worn by him again or worn by someone else; and it has been said he was so called because he scattered the Azd through the lands — his brother ʿImrān was a soothsayer. A soothsayer woman called Ẓarīfa came to him and told him of the approaching ruin of the dam and the overflow of the torrent, and warned him. So he gathered the people of Maʾrib, made food for them, and told them about the torrent, and they agreed to emigrate. His brother ʿImrān said to them: "I will describe lands to you; choose whichever of them you wish. Whoever of you has far-reaching ambition and a camel that does not bolt, let him go to the ravine of Karūd" — and Hamdān went there. Then he said: "Whoever of you has statecraft and patience in the crises of fortune, let him go to Baṭn Murr" — and Khuzāʿa went there. Then he said: "Whoever of you wants [palms] firmly rooted in the mud that feed in time of drought, let him go to Yathrib of the palms" — and al-Aws and al-Khazraj settled there. Then he said: "Whoever of you wants wine and leaven, command and the conferring of command, let him go to Buṣrā and Sadīr" — which are in the land of Syria — and Ghassān settled there. Then he said: "Whoever of you wants fine garments, noble horses, gold and silver coin (awrāq), let him go to Iraq" — and Mālik ibn Fahm ibn al-Azd went there. Mālik ibn al-Yamān stayed behind among his people until the torrent drove them out; they settled in Najrān and traced their descent to Madhḥij. A group of them entered among Maʿadd, but Maʿadd drove them out after wars, and they settled in the mountains of al-Sharāt on the borders of Syria. When they dispersed through the lands in this way, the Arabs coined the proverb about them, saying: "They went off like the hands of Sabā" (ayday sabā and ayādī sabā).

dervis-irab:89-93.t:
* I'rab:
(مَنْ جاءَ بِالْحَسَنَةِ فَلَهُ خَيْرٌ مِنْها وَهُمْ مِنْ فَزَعٍ يَوْمَئِذٍ آمِنُونَ): resumptive speech, introduced to pave the way for the close of the sūra by summarising the destiny of the doer of good and the doer of evil. (من) is a conditional noun that puts in the jussive, a mubtadaʾ (subject); (بالحسنة) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (جاء), or to an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial), the bāʾ then being for accompaniment (mulābasa), i.e. he came bearing it. The fāʾ is a linking particle; (له) is a fronted khabar (predicate) and (خير) a postponed mubtadaʾ; (منها) is an adjective of (خير), or attached to it, taking it as an elative (ism tafḍīl). (هم) is a mubtadaʾ; (من فزع) is attached to (آمنون), and (آمنون) is the khabar. (يوم) is an adverb annexed to one like it [i.e. إذ], and it is attached to an omitted adjective of (فزع), i.e. "occurring on that day". It was read with (فزع) annexed to (يومئذ).
(وَمَنْ جاءَ بِالسَّيِّئَةِ فَكُبَّتْ وُجُوهُهُمْ فِي النَّارِ هَلْ تُجْزَوْنَ إِلَّا ما كُنْتُمْ تَعْمَلُونَ): the wāw is a conjunction; (من) is conditional; (جاء بالسيئة) is the protasis (fiʿl al-sharṭ). The fāʾ is a linking particle entering upon an omitted «قد», i.e. «فقد كبت», so that the apodosis may properly be joined with it. (كبت) is a passive past verb and (وجوههم) is the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent); (في النار) is attached to (كبت); the clause (فكبت) is in the position of the jussive as the apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ). (هل) is an interrogative particle; (تجزون) is a passive imperfect verb, nominative (marfūʿ) by the retention of the nūn, by way of iltifāt (shift of person); the wāw is the nāʾib fāʿil; and the clause is a ḥāl, i.e. "and their faces are cast down, it being said to them: Are you recompensed …?" (إلا) is a particle of restriction; (ما) is the second object of (تجزون); the clause (كنتم) is the ṣila (relative clause); (كان) and its noun, and the clause (تعملون) is its khabar.
(إِنَّما أُمِرْتُ أَنْ أَعْبُدَ رَبَّ هذِهِ الْبَلْدَةِ الَّذِي حَرَّمَها): the clause is the object of an omitted saying, i.e. "Say to them: I have only been commanded". (إنما) is the restraining particle and what it restrains (kāffa wa-makfūfa); (أمرت) is a passive past verb and the tāʾ is the nāʾib fāʿil; (أن أعبد) is in the sense of a maṣdar (verbal noun) that is accusative by removal of the preposition, and the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to (أمرت). (رب) is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object); (هذه) is annexed to (رب); (البلدة) is a badal (substitute) of the demonstrative, and what is meant by it is Mecca, may Allah guard it; (الذي) is a naʿt (adjective) of (رب هذه البلدة), and the clause (حرمها) is the ṣila. (وَلَهُ كُلُّ شَيْءٍ وَأُمِرْتُ أَنْ أَكُونَ مِنَ الْمُسْلِمِينَ): the wāw is circumstantial; (له) is a fronted khabar and (كل شيء) a postponed mubtadaʾ; the secret of this ḥāl will come in the Rhetoric section. (أمرت) is conjoined to the first (أمرت), and (أن أكون من المسلمين) is also conjoined to what precedes. (وَأَنْ أَتْلُوَا الْقُرْآنَ فَمَنِ اهْتَدى فَإِنَّما يَهْتَدِي لِنَفْسِهِ): (وأن أتلو) is conjoined to (أن أكون), i.e. "and I have been commanded to recite"; (القرآن) is the direct object. In (فمن) the fāʾ is for drawing a consequence (tafrīʿiyya) and (من) is conditional, a mubtadaʾ; (اهتدى) is a past verb in the position of the jussive as the protasis; the fāʾ is a linking particle; (إنما) is kāffa wa-makfūfa; (يهتدي) is an imperfect verb whose fāʿil (agent) is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "he"; the fāʾ is a linking particle; (إنما) is kāffa wa-makfūfa; (يهتدي) is an imperfect verb in the nominative whose agent is latent, its implied form being "he"; (لنفسه) is attached to (يهتدي). [Translator's note: the source repeats the parsing of «فإنما يهتدي» twice; translated as written.] (وَمَنْ ضَلَّ فَقُلْ إِنَّما أَنَا مِنَ الْمُنْذِرِينَ): conjoined to the preceding clause and parallel to it in its parsing; a verb of request must be supplied after the fāʾ, i.e. "then say to him: I am only one of the warners". (وَقُلِ الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ سَيُرِيكُمْ آياتِهِ فَتَعْرِفُونَها وَما رَبُّكَ بِغافِلٍ عَمَّا تَعْمَلُونَ): the wāw is a conjunction; (قل) is an imperative verb whose agent is latent, its implied form being "you"; (الحمد) is a mubtadaʾ and (لله) the khabar, and the clause is the object of saying (maqūl al-qawl). In (سيريكم) the sīn is a particle of the future; (يريكم) is an imperfect verb, the kāf is the first direct object and (آياته) the second direct object; the clause is part of the completion of the object of saying, falling within its thread. In (فتعرفونها) the fāʾ is a conjunction, and (تعرفونها) is an imperfect verb, an agent and a direct object. The wāw is a conjunction; (ما) is the Ḥijāzī negative; (ربك) is its noun; in (بغافل) the bāʾ is a redundant preposition and (غافل) is genitive in wording and accusative in position because it is the khabar of (ما); (عما) is attached to (غافل), and the clause (تعملون) is the ṣila.

* Rhetoric:
Guarding (al-iḥtirās):
In the saying of the Exalted «وله كل شيء» there is a fine iḥtirās. Mention of this device has preceded, and that it is brought to ward off a misconception that the speech might give rise to. He, Glorified is He, annexed His name to Mecca to honour it and mention its sanctity; and since He annexed His name to the town singled out with this honour, He followed that by annexing everything else to His dominion, to cut off the misconception that His dominion is restricted to the town referred to, and to draw attention to the fact that the first annexation was meant only for honouring, not because it alone is the dominion of Allah the Exalted.
Al-Bāqillānī analyses Sūrat al-Naml:
Furthermore, at the close of this sūra we would like to make a quick, analytical reference to the book «Iʿjāz al-Qur'an» by Abū Bakr al-Bāqillānī, whose fame has spread among people. It combines with its theological (kalām) spirit a literary character, since in treating inimitability he did not restrict himself to studying it from the theological side, but addressed the aspect of eloquence and style. The orator al-Bāqillānī grew up skilled in disputation, of high standing in the sciences of the Qur'an, the Sunna and theology; he confronted many opponents and dissenters and battled them with proofs, and he debated the scholars of the Byzantines, which aroused the admiration of his contemporaries for him.
The king ʿAḍud al-Dawla sent him to the king of the Byzantines in the year 371 AH on an official embassy. Once, while he was in the Byzantine capital, they brought him in to some priests, and the Qāḍī said to the priest: "How are you, and your wife and children?" The Byzantine was astonished and said to him: "The one who sent you mentioned in the letter of credence that you are the tongue of the community and foremost among the scholars of the religion; did you not know that the metropolitans and monks are above having wives and children?" The Qāḍī Abū Bakr answered him: "We have seen that you do not hold Allah, Glorified is He, above having a wife and children; are the metropolitans with you holier, more majestic and more exalted than Allah, Glorified is He?" The chief of the Byzantines wanted to disgrace the Qāḍī, so he said to him: "Tell me about the story of ʿĀʾisha, the wife of your Prophet, and what was said about her." He answered him: "They are two women about whom was said what was said: the wife of our Prophet and Mary the mother of the Messiah. As for the wife of our Prophet, she did not give birth; and as for Mary, she came with a child carrying him on her shoulders; and Allah declared both of them innocent of what they were accused of." The Byzantine was silenced and could give no answer.
Summary of al-Bāqillānī's theory of inimitability:
1- He begins by presenting the idea in a simple presentation: he establishes the soundness of the text of the Qur'an we have in our hands, that it is truly the Book of Allah revealed to His Prophet, and that it is Muḥammad's sign and his everlasting miracle.
2- He establishes the incapacity of the Arabs to produce its like despite its challenging them repeatedly.
3- From the preceding premises he arrives at a general conclusion which is the summary of his theory of inimitability, namely «the departure of the composition (naẓm) of the Qur'an from all the speech of the Arabs and their compositions». He then explains this theory in the book of inimitability, saying: «The third aspect is that it is novel in composition, marvellous in arrangement, reaching the utmost in eloquence through the variety of its aspects and the diversity of its ways, departing from what is familiar in the composition of all their speech, differing from what is customary in the arrangement of their discourse; it has a style peculiar to it and is distinguished in its sections from the styles of ordinary speech.»
Before entering into the composition of the Qur'an and the analysis of its sūras, he takes up an ode of Imruʾ al-Qays and another of al-Buḥturī, to sketch his method in criticism and the application of his approach. In both odes he moves from the opening to the end, drawing attention to aspects of beauty and points of weakness. In his analysis of the ode of Imruʾ al-Qays — or his Muʿallaqa, more correctly — he weighs what it contains of the arts of expression, variation in speech and composition of discourse against what is similar or close to it in the Qur'an, always drawing attention to the superiority of the Qur'an. Personal criticism often entered into al-Bāqillānī's opinion in analysing the Muʿallaqa of Imruʾ al-Qays, even where that opinion contradicted the opinions of all the critics. Look at him, how he faults the poet in his saying:
إذا قامتا تضوع المسك منهما ...
(When the two of them rose, musk wafted from them …)
He says: «The aspect of affectation in it is his saying "When the two of them rose, musk wafted from them"; had he wished to do well, he would have conveyed that there was fragrance about them in every state; as for only in the state of rising, that is a shortcoming.» This is an evident prejudice by Abū Bakr against the poet and the meaning he treated; for there is no doubt that in this expression there is a fine artistic touch resting on the word «قامتا», because it is the source of motion and life in the whole picture: it shows you the two girls coming and going, their thin garments giving off perfume which spreads through their sides, and the air becomes fragrant with its scent from what motion stirs in the air, carrying the perfume to the noses to inhale it; and that is not possible in sitting and stillness. Nevertheless, we do not deny some of the slips in the creed [Translator's note: so in the source, «العقيدة»; the context suggests «القصيدة», "the ode"] to which al-Bāqillānī drew attention; rather we adopt his opinion and appreciate his depth and fine deduction. Listen to this marvellous criticism that silences tongues. He took up the opening of the Muʿallaqa in the first two verses, which are:
فقا نبك من ذكرى حبيب ومنزل ... بسقط اللوى بين الدخول فحومل
فتوضح فالمقراة لم يعف رسمها ... لما نسجتها من خبوب وشمائل
(Halt, you two, let us weep at the remembrance of a beloved and an abode at the edge of the sand-dune between al-Dakhūl and Ḥawmal, and Tūḍiḥ and al-Miqrāt — its traces not effaced, for what the south and north winds have woven over it.)
And he said: «He was not content with mentioning one boundary until he had defined it by four boundaries, as if he wanted to sell the abode and feared that, if he omitted a boundary, his sale would be invalid or his condition void.»
In his analysis of al-Buḥturī's ode there are some artistic niceties in criticism, which we summarise as follows:
1- Poetic vision: he pointed to its disorder in al-Buḥturī in his likening the phantom to lightning, in al-Buḥturī's saying:
أهلا بذلكم الخيال المقبل ... فعل الذي نهواه أم لم يفعل
برق سرى من بطن وجرة فاهتدت ... بسناه أعناق الركاب الضلل
(Welcome to that approaching phantom, whether it did what we desire or did not — lightning that travelled by night from the hollow of Wajra, by whose gleam the necks of the straying mounts found their way.)
He said: «He made the phantom like lightning because of the brightness of its night journey»; and in his view the phantom is not to be likened to lightning, because lightning is swift and flashing, while the phantom travels as the breeze travels.
2- Padding (al-ḥashw): it is the excess of wording over the required meaning, and it is a defect in composition.
3- Triteness in the figurative image, such as simile, metaphor or metonymy.
4- Verbal lustre: he sees in some of al-Buḥturī's verses lustre and charm, and sees in others a lack of freshness and lustre.
5- Disorder in meaning: of this is his saying in criticising some verses: «The mention of the censurers ran in a way to which this verse does not connect and with which it does not accord; then what he mentioned of waiting, though pretty in wording, is affected in meaning, because one who stands in the abode does not wait for something, but only stands in grief, humility and bewilderment.» These are the verses the criticism treated:
ما الحسن عندك يا سعاد بمحسن ... فيما أتاه ولا الجمال بمجمل
عذل المشوق وإن من سيما الهوى ... في حيث تجهله لجاج العاذل
ماذا عليك من انتظار متيم ... بل ما يضرك وفقة في منزل إن سيل عيّ عن الجواب فلم يطق ... رجعا فكيف يكون إن لم يسأل
(Beauty in you, O Suʿād, does not do good in what it does, nor does loveliness act kindly. The longing one was blamed — and among the marks of passion, where you do not know it, is the censurer's persistence. What harm to you is the waiting of one enslaved by love — nay, what harms you in a pause at an abode? If he is asked, he is too tongue-tied to answer and cannot reply; so how would it be if he were not asked?)
6- Enjambment (al-taḍmīn): it is a defect known among Arab critics.
7- Departing from the structure of the ancient Arabic ode.
8- Complexity and lack of smoothness in arranging and casting the words, which is a defect in formulation and composition.
9- The opening and its connection with disjunction and conjunction (al-faṣl wal-waṣl).
10- Sharing of meanings between him and other poets, with variation in excellence.
11- The construction and arrangement of the phrase, and its variation between sound and disturbed composition.
Analysis of Sūrat al-Naml:
Al-Bāqillānī takes up the sūra as a whole: he explains its rare words and shows its beauty of wording and meaning, and he begins analysing it from its start, saying: «He began with mentioning the sūra up to His making clear that the Qur'an is from Him; then He joined to that the story of Moses, and that he saw a fire and said to his family «امكثوا إني آنست نارا سآتيكم منها بشهاب قبس لعلكم تصطلون», and He said in Sūrat Ṭā Hā in this story: «لعلي آتيكم منها بقبس أو أجد على النار هدى». Then He said: «فلما جاءها نودي أن بورك من في النار ومن حولها وسبحان الله رب العالمين». Look at what He made the first speech run towards, how it connected with that introduction, and how He joined to it what follows of reports about Lordship, and what indicated it, of the transformation of eloquence [Translator's note: so in the source, «قلب الفصاحة»; presumably «قلب العصا», "the transformation of the staff", is meant], making it a proof guiding him to Him and a miracle leading him to Him. Look at the single words standing by themselves in beauty and in the noble meanings they contain; then at what He paired with this sign and joined to this proof, the white hand, from the light of the proof, without harm. Then look at verse after verse and word after word: do you find it as we described, of marvellous composition and novel description? Every word, were it taken alone, would be the utmost in beauty and a sign in indication; so how much more when its sisters are joined to it and its kind are combined with it, running in beauty its course and taking up its meaning; then from story to story and from chapter to chapter without any flaw occurring in the composition from section to section, until the section is depicted for you as a connection, by novel arrangement and eloquent revelation.»
Al-Bāqillānī shows the superiority of the composition of the Qur'an over ordinary speech: he invites one to imitate it, and he attains nothing and admits incapacity before the wording and composition of the Qur'an. He continues analysing the sūra, saying: «When could it be prepared for a human being to say, in describing the letter of Solomon, peace be upon him, after mentioning the address and the basmala, this lofty, noble word «ألّا تعلوا علي وأتوني مسلمين»; and to pass from that to what she arrived at of management and what she occupied herself with of consultation, and her magnifying the matter of the one consulted, and their magnifying her matter and obedience to her, with those novel words and marvellous expressions; then her speech after that — so that you know the firmness of her saying: «يا أيها الملأ أفتوني في أمري ما كنت قاطعة أمرا حتى تشهدون»; and He mentioned their saying: «قالوا نحن أولو قوة وأولوا بأس شديد والأمر إليك فانظري ماذا تأمرين» — you will not find in their description of themselves anything more novel than how He described them. His saying «الأمر إليك» — you know its excellence in itself, its marvellous meaning and the place of its precision in this speech, and the firmness of the verse-ending and its fitness for what precedes it, namely His saying: «فانظري ماذا تأمرين». Then [look] at this brevity, and at the clarity together with the inimitability; for speech may be spoiled by brevity and obscured by lightening and concision, but this is something that brevity only makes more expansive, because of its firmness and its falling in its proper place» — until he says: «If I were to explain to you what is in every verse, the matter would become long for you; but by what I have explained I have made clear, and by what I have detailed I have established, the way I have followed, the direction I intended, the aim at which I aimed and the path to which I have called.»
We reckon that after this you have become acquainted with the book on inimitability, for we have cited for you the best of what is in it.

dervis-irab:27-33.t:
* Vocabulary:
(أَفْتُونِي): advise me. «الفتوى» is the answer concerning an incident; it was derived by way of metaphor from «الفتا» (youth) in age. What is meant by «الفتوى» here is their advising her with what they had, as we mentioned, concerning the opinion and plan that occurred to her. In al-Asās: «So-and-so is one of the people of fatwā and futyā; "come, let us go to judgment" (فتعالوا ففاتونا) [Translator's note: so in the source]; and «تفاتوا إليه»: they referred their dispute to him for judgment. Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said:
هلمّ إلى قضاة الغوث فاسأل ... برهطك والبيان لدى القضاة
(Come to the judges of al-Ghawth and ask about your clan; clear proof lies with the judges.)
أنخ بفناء أشدق من عديّ ... ومن جرم وهم أهل التفاتي
(Make your camel kneel in the courtyard of an eloquent man of ʿAdī and of Jarm, for they are the people to whom disputes are referred.)
And ʿUmar ibn Abī Rabīʿa said:
فبتّ أفاتيها فلا هي ترعوي ... بجود ولا تبدي إباء فتبخلا
(I spent the night questioning her, and she neither relented with generosity nor showed refusal so as to be miserly.)
i.e., I asked her.»
The fāʾ may be given ḍamma or fatḥa [i.e., futwā and fatwā], as stated in Adab al-Kātib by Ibn Qutayba, who said: «They said: fatwā and futyā, baqwā and buqyā, thanwā and thunyā, raʿwā and ruʿyā.»
(أُولُوا قُوَّةٍ): a collective noun (ism jamʿ) meaning "possessors"; its singular is «ذو» meaning "possessor". It has also been said that it is the plural of «ذو» not from its own wording. It has been stated before that it is among the words annexed to (treated like) the sound masculine plural. The feminine is «أولات», whose singular is «ذات»; you say: «جاء أولو العلم وأولات الفضل» (the men of knowledge and the women of merit came).

* I'rab:
(قالَ سَنَنْظُرُ أَصَدَقْتَ أَمْ كُنْتَ مِنَ الْكاذِبِينَ): resumptive speech, brought to answer a question arising from the hoopoe's account. The clause «سننظر» is the object of the saying (maqūl al-qawl). The hamza is interrogative; «صدقت» is a verb and its fāʿil (agent); «أم» is connective (muttaṣila), balancing the hamza; «كان» and its noun, and «من الكاذبين» its khabar (predicate). He turned from the verb corresponding to what preceded it to the noun for a rhetorical point indicated more than once before, namely making him one [Translator's note: the source prints «واحد» for «واحدا»] of the group branded with lying.
(اذْهَبْ بِكِتابِي هذا فَأَلْقِهْ إِلَيْهِمْ ثُمَّ تَوَلَّ عَنْهُمْ فَانْظُرْ ماذا يَرْجِعُونَ): some omitted speech must be implied so that the events of the story fit together, i.e.: then it showed them the water, and they drew it out, quenched their thirst, made ablution and prayed. Then Solomon wrote a letter, of this form: "From the servant of Allah Solomon to Bilqīs, queen of Sabaʾ. In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Peace be upon whoever follows guidance. To proceed: do not exalt yourselves against me, and come to me in submission." Then he sealed it with his seal, then said to the hoopoe: "Go." So the clause is the object of an omitted saying. «اذهب» is an imperative verb whose agent is latent (mustatir), its implied form being "anta" (you); «بكتابي» are attached to (mutaʿalliq) «اذهب»; «هذا» is a naʿt (adjective) of «كتابي» or a badal (substitute) of it. «فألقه»: the fāʾ is a conjunction; «ألقه» is an imperative verb, a latent agent and a mafʿūl bihi (direct object); «إليهم» are attached to «ألقه» [Translator's note: the source prints «وأنهم متعلقان بألفه», evidently misprints for «وإليهم متعلقان بألقه»]. «ثم» is a conjunction; «تول» is an imperative verb [indeclinable] on the dropping of the weak letter, its agent latent, its implied form being "anta"; «عنهم» are attached to an omitted ḥāl (circumstantial), i.e., passing beyond them to a nearby place where you can hide, so that what they say is within your hearing. «فانظر» is conjoined to «تول». «ماذا يرجعون»: in this expression there are two views:
The first: that «انظر» means "consider and reflect". Then «ماذا» is an interrogative noun in the position of accusative as a fronted object of «يرجعون», its implied sense being "what thing do they return"; or you make «ما» an interrogative noun, a mubtadaʾ (subject), and «ذا» a relative noun meaning "that which", the khabar of «ما», the clause «يرجعون» being the ṣila (relative clause) of «ذا», with the returning pronoun omitted, its implied sense being "what is the thing that they return?" On both determinations, the governing word, «انظر», has been suspended (muʿallaq) from the interrogative clause by the interrogative, so its position is accusative by removal of the preposition, i.e., "look into such-and-such and reflect on it".
The second: that «انظر» means "wait", as in the words of the Exalted «انظرونا نقتبس من نوركم». Then «ماذا» as a whole is a relative noun — one of the uses of «ماذا» that will come in the Benefits section — and it is the direct object, i.e., "wait for what they return"; the clause «يرجعون» is the ṣila, and the returning pronoun is omitted, as stated. The meaning is: what answer they give back, or what words they exchange with one another.
(قالَتْ يا أَيُّهَا الْمَلَأُ إِنِّي أُلْقِيَ إِلَيَّ كِتابٌ كَرِيمٌ): some omitted speech must be implied, in whose omission concision was observed. Its implied form, as Muqātil said: «The hoopoe carried the letter in its beak and flew until it stopped over the woman's head, with the soldiers and armies around her. It fluttered for a while as the people watched; the woman raised her head, and it dropped the letter into her lap.» More reports concerning the determination of this omitted part will come.
«وإني»: «إن» and its noun; the clause «ألقي» is its khabar; «إليّ» are attached to «ألقي»; «كتاب» is the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent) and «كريم» an adjective. The secret of this description will come in the Rhetoric section.
(إِنَّهُ مِنْ سُلَيْمانَ وَإِنَّهُ بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ): the clause is resumptive, brought to answer an implied question, as if they said: "From whom is it, and what does it contain?" So she said: it is from Solomon. «إن» and its noun, and «من سليمان» its khabar. «وإنه»: the wāw is a conjunction; «إن» and its noun, and the clause of the basmala is its khabar. The i'rab of the basmala was given at the beginning of this book.
(أَلَّا تَعْلُوا عَلَيَّ وَأْتُونِي مُسْلِمِينَ): «أن» is explicative (mufassira), what it explains being «كتاب», because it includes the meaning of saying without its letters. «لا» is the prohibitive lā, «تعلوا» an imperfect verb, jussive (majzūm) by «لا», the wāw is the agent, and «عليّ» are attached to «تعلوا». «أن» may also be maṣdariyya, making the verb accusative, with «لا» negative; «أن» with what falls in its scope is then an interpreted maṣdar, in the position of nominative as a badal of «كتاب», or as the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e., "its content is that you not exalt yourselves"; or in the position of accusative by removal of the preposition, i.e., «بأن لا تعلوا». «وأتوني»: the wāw is a conjunction; «ائتوني» is an imperative verb, indeclinable (mabnī) on the dropping of the nūn; the wāw is the agent, the nūn is the nūn of protection (wiqāya), and the yāʾ is the direct object. «مسلمين» is a ḥāl.
(قالَتْ يا أَيُّهَا الْمَلَأُ أَفْتُونِي فِي أَمْرِي): «أفتوني» is an imperative verb, indeclinable on the dropping of the nūn; the wāw is the agent, the nūn is of protection and the yāʾ is the direct object; «في أمري» are attached to «أفتوني».
(ما كُنْتُ قاطِعَةً أَمْراً حَتَّى تَشْهَدُونِ): «ما» is negative; «كنت قاطعة»: «كان», its noun and its khabar; «أمرا» is the direct object. «حتى» is a particle of limit and a preposition; «تشهدون» is an imperfect verb, accusative by an implied «أن» after «حتى», the sign of its accusative being the dropping of the nūn; the nūn present is the nūn of protection, and the omitted yāʾ of the speaker is the direct object.
(قالُوا نَحْنُ أُولُوا قُوَّةٍ وَأُولُوا بَأْسٍ شَدِيدٍ): the clause «نحن» is the object of the saying; «نحن» is a mubtadaʾ and «أولو» its khabar, the sign of its nominative being the wāw because it is annexed to the sound masculine plural; «قوة» is muḍāf ilayhi; «وأولو بأس شديد» is conjoined to what preceded.
(وَالْأَمْرُ إِلَيْكِ فَانْظُرِي ماذا تَأْمُرِينَ): the wāw is a conjunction; «الأمر» is a mubtadaʾ and «إليك» its khabar, i.e., it is entrusted to you and we obey you. «فانظري»: the fāʾ is the fāʾ al-faṣīḥa, because it discloses something implied, as if they imagined that she might be desirous of fighting, or that they were desirous of it: "if you want that and are resolved to plunge into war, we are experts at it (abnāʾ bajdatihā)". «انظري» means "reflect". «ماذا» is an interrogative noun — its i'rab has preceded and its uses will come — and here it is in the position of accusative as a fronted object of «تأمرين»; the interrogative suspends the [verb of] considering.

* Rhetoric:
In this dialogue that took place between Bilqīs and the chiefs of her people, and in the description of Solomon's letter after mentioning the address and the basmala, there are numerous arts, the most important of which we give below:
1- Ishāra (allusion):
This art has been referred to earlier in this book. Qudāma derived it from the harmony of wording with meaning and explained it, saying: it is that a little wording indicates much meaning, so that the indication of the wording is like pointing with the hand, which by one movement points to many things. The difference between it and ījāz (concision) is that ījāz uses the words assigned to the meaning, while the words of ishāra are a quick, indicative glimpse; so the indication of wording in ījāz is indication by correspondence (dalālat muṭābaqa), while the indication of wording in ishāra is either indication by inclusion (taḍammun) or indication by entailment (iltizām); the indication here is by inclusion. She described Solomon's letter as noble (karīm) because it came from a noble king, or because it was sealed. In a ḥadīth it is reported from him ﷺ that he said: "The nobility of a letter is its seal." And from Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ: whoever writes a letter to his brother and does not seal it has made light of him.
It is related that she was asleep; when she slept, she would lock the doors and put the keys under her head. The hoopoe entered through a window-opening and dropped the letter on her throat while she lay on her back — it has also been said that it pecked her — and she woke up alarmed. When she saw the seal she trembled and said to her people what she said.
2- Ījāz (concision):
In their words «قالوا نحن أولو قوة وأولو بأس شديد والأمر إليك فانظري ماذا تأمرين» there is a wonderful concision. First, it indicates the magnifying of consultation and Bilqīs's magnifying the standing of the one consulted; second, it indicates their magnifying her command and obeying her. In their words «والأمر إليك» and «فانظري ماذا تأمرين» there is a concision that intoxicates minds. Abū Bakr Muḥammad ibn al-Ṭayyib al-Bāqillānī said in his book Iʿjāz al-Qur'an: «Speech may be spoiled by abridgement and obscured by lightening and concision; but this is among what abridgement only expands, because of its firmness and its falling in its proper place, and its concision contains a versatility that goes beyond its place and position» — until he says: «You will find in all that we have recited to you only what, when expanded, gives benefit, and when abridged is complete and excellent in its kind; and when the wise man lets the glance of his thought roam over its sides, and the learned man sends the eyes of his inquiries into its edges, they fall only upon beauties following one another and marvels coming in succession.»

* Benefits:
Ibn Hishām devoted a section of al-Mughnī to «ماذا», which we summarize below, parsing its examples:
«ماذا» comes in Arabic in several ways:
1- That «ما» is interrogative and «ذا» a demonstrative, as in «ماذا التواني؟» (what is this slackness?) and «ماذا الوقوف؟» (what is this standing still?). «ما» is an interrogative noun, a mubtadaʾ, and «ذا» its khabar; «التواني» is a badal or ʿaṭf bayān (explicative apposition), i.e., "what thing is this slackness?"
2- That «ما» is interrogative and «ذا» a relative, as in the words of Labīd:
ألا تسألان المرء ماذا يحاول ... أنحب فيقضي أم ضلال وباطل
(Will you two not ask a man what it is he strives for: a vow he fulfils, or error and vanity?)
«ما» is an interrogative noun, a mubtadaʾ; «ذا» is a relative noun, its khabar; the clause «يحاول» is the ṣila; the hamza is interrogative, and «نحب» is a badal of «ما».
3- That «ماذا» as a whole is an interrogative, by compounding, as when you say «لماذا جئت؟» (why did you come?), and the poet's words:
يا خزر تغلب ماذا بال نسوتكم ... لا يستفقن إلى الديرين تحنانا
(O squint-eyed ones of Taghlib, what is the matter with your women, that they never recover from longing for the two monasteries?)
«ماذا» is a compound interrogative noun, a mubtadaʾ, and «بال نسوتكم» its khabar.
4- That «ماذا» as a whole is a generic noun meaning "a thing", or a relative meaning "that which", according to a disagreement over the interpretation of the poet's words:
دعي ماذا علمت سأتقيه ... ولكن بالمغيّب نبئيني
(Leave aside what you know — I shall guard against it — but tell me of what is hidden.)
The majority hold that «ماذا» as a whole is the object of «دعي»; then they differed: it has been said that it is a relative meaning "that which", and it has been said that it is an indefinite noun meaning "a thing". There are two other ways which Ibn Hishām mentioned, but we saw no need for them because they do not occur in eloquent speech.
